nodes.summary: The authors report observing entropic precursors expected of emergent gravity after introducing non-stabilizerness into their holographic-code model.

sources.title: Observation of gravity-like signatures in holographic codes on a quantum computer

nodes.label: Wormhole-like entropic behavior in a quantum code
nodes.summary: The authors report constructing and measuring a quantum code whose entropic behavior resembles that of a highly quantum wormhole.

sources.title: Observation of gravity-like signatures in holographic codes on a quantum computer

nodes.label: Nearly simultaneous arrival of widely separated photon energies from GRB 090510
nodes.summary: NASA reports that two photons from GRB 090510, differing in energy by a factor of one million, arrived at Fermi nearly simultaneously after traveling more than 7.3 billion light-years.

sources.title: Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope: Gamma-ray Bursts

nodes.label: GRB 090510 constraint on energy-dependent light speed
nodes.summary: NASA reports that GRB 090510 placed a strong constraint on variation of light speed with photon energy, with high- and low-energy gamma rays arriving within one second after traveling approximately seven billion light-years.

sources.title: Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope: Gamma-ray Bursts

nodes.label: Fermi GBM detector coverage and burst detection rate
nodes.summary: NASA describes the Fermi Gamma-ray Burst Monitor as having 14 detectors covering the unobscured sky, detecting approximately 240 gamma-ray bursts per year across an energy range of 8 keV to 40 MeV.

sources.title: Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope: Gamma-ray Bursts

nodes.label: algorithm
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines algorithm as: A computable set of steps to achieve a desired result.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: algorithm

nodes.label: data structure
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines data structure as: An organization of information, usually in memory, for better algorithm efficiency , such as queue , stack , linked list , heap , dictionary , and tree , or conceptual unity, such as the name and address of a person. It may include redundant information, such as length of the list or number of nodes in a subtree .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: dataStructure

nodes.label: search
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines search as: Look for a value or item in a data structure. There are dozens of algorithms, data structures, and approaches.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: search

nodes.label: sort
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines sort as: Arrange items in a predetermined order. There are dozens of algorithms, the choice of which depends on factors such as the number of items relative to working memory, knowledge of the orderliness of the items or the range of the keys , the cost of comparing keys vs. the cost of moving items, etc. Most algorithms can be implemented as an in-place sort , and many can be implemented so they are stable , too. Formal Definition: The sort operation may be defined in terms of an initial array, S, of N items and a final array, S′, as follows. S′ i ≤ S′ i+1 , 0 < i < N (the items are in order) and S′ is a permutation of S.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: sort

nodes.label: binary search
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines binary search as: Search a sorted array by repeatedly dividing the search interval in half. Begin with an interval covering the whole array. If the value of the search key is less than the item in the middle of the interval, narrow the interval to the lower half. Otherwise narrow it to the upper half. Repeatedly check until the value is found or the interval is empty.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: binarySearch

nodes.label: linear search
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines linear search as: Search an array or list by checking items one at a time. Also known as sequential search.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: linearSearch

nodes.label: merge sort
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines merge sort as: A sort algorithm that splits the items to be sorted into two groups, recursively sorts each group, and merges them into a final, sorted sequence. Run time is Θ (n log n).

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: mergesort

nodes.label: quicksort
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines quicksort as: Pick an element from the array (the pivot), partition the remaining elements into those greater than and less than this pivot, and recursively sort the partitions. There are many variants of the basic scheme above: to select the pivot, to partition the array, to stop the recursion or switch to another algorithm for small partitions, etc.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: quicksort

nodes.label: heapsort
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines heapsort as: A sort algorithm that builds a heap , then repeatedly extracts the maximum item. Run time is O(n log n) .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: heapSort

nodes.label: insertion sort
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines insertion sort as: Sort by repeatedly taking the next item and inserting it into the final data structure in its proper order with respect to items already inserted. Run time is O(n 2 ) because of moves. Also known as linear insertion sort.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: insertionSort

nodes.label: selection sort
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines selection sort as: A sort algorithm that repeatedly searches remaining items to find the least one and moves it to its final location. The run time is Θ(n²) , where n is the number of elements. The number of swaps is O(n) .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: selectionSort

nodes.label: bubble sort
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines bubble sort as: Sort by comparing each adjacent pair of items in a list in turn, swapping the items if necessary, and repeating the pass through the list until no swaps are done. Also known as sinking sort, exchange sort.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bubblesort

nodes.label: counting sort
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines counting sort as: A 2-pass sort algorithm that is efficient when the number of distinct keys is small compared to the number of items. The first pass counts the occurrences of each key in an auxiliary array , and then makes a running total so each auxiliary entry is the number of preceding keys. The second pass puts each item in its final place according to the auxiliary entry for that key.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: countingsort

nodes.label: radix sort
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines radix sort as: A multiple pass distribution sort algorithm that distributes each item to a bucket according to part of the item's key beginning with the least significant part of the key. After each pass, items are collected from the buckets, keeping the items in order, then redistributed according to the next most significant part of the key.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: radixsort

nodes.label: bucket sort
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines bucket sort as: A distribution sort where input elements are initially distributed to several buckets based on an interpolation of the element's key . Each bucket is sorted if necessary, and the buckets' contents are concatenated. Also known as bin sort.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bucketsort

nodes.label: bintree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines bintree as: A regular decomposition k-d tree for region data.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bintree

nodes.label: binary search tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines binary search tree as: A binary tree where every node's left subtree has keys less than the node's key, and every right subtree has keys greater than the node's key.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: binarySearchTree

nodes.label: AVL tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines AVL tree as: A balanced binary search tree where the height of the two subtrees ( children ) of a node differs by at most one. Look-up, insertion, and deletion are O(log n) , where n is the number of nodes in the tree.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: avltree

nodes.label: red-black tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines red-black tree as: A nearly-balanced tree that uses an extra bit per node to maintain balance. No leaf is more than twice as far from the root as any other. Formal Definition: A red-black tree with n internal nodes has height at most 2log 2 (n+1). Also known as symmetric binary B-tree.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: redblack

nodes.label: heap
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines heap as: A complete tree where every node has a key more extreme (greater or less) than or equal to the key of its parent . Usually understood to be a binary heap .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: heap

nodes.label: queue
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines queue as: A collection of items in which only the earliest added item may be accessed. Basic operations are add (to the tail ) or enqueue and delete (from the head ) or dequeue. Delete returns the item removed. Also known as "first-in, first-out" or FIFO. Formal Definition: It is convenient to define delete or dequeue in terms of remove and a new operation, front. The operations new(), add(v, Q), front(Q), and remove(Q) may be defined with axiomatic semantics as follows. new() returns a queue front(add(v, new())) = v remove(add(v, new())) = new() front(add(v, add(w, Q))) = front(add(w, Q)) remove(add(v, add(w, Q))) = add(v, remove(add(w, Q))) where Q is a queue and v and w are values. Also known as FIFO.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: queue

nodes.label: stack
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines stack as: A collection of items in which only the most recently added item may be removed. The latest added item is at the top. Basic operations are push and pop. Often top and isEmpty are available, too. Also known as "last-in, first-out" or LIFO. Formal Definition: The operations new(), push(v, S), top(S), and popoff(S) may be defined with axiomatic semantics as follows. new() returns a stack popoff(push(v, S)) = S top(push(v, S)) = v where S is a stack and v is a value. The pop operation is a combination of top, to return the top value, and popoff, to remove the top value. The predicate isEmpty(S) may be defined with the following additional axioms. isEmpty(new()) = true isEmpty(push(v, S)) = false Also known as LIFO.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: stack

nodes.label: linked list
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines linked list as: A list implemented by each item having a link to the next item. Also known as singly linked list.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: linkedList

nodes.label: doubly linked list
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines doubly linked list as: A variant of a linked list in which each item has a link to the previous item as well as the next. This allows easily accessing list items backward as well as forward and deleting any item in constant time. Also known as two-way linked list, symmetrically linked list.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: doublyLinkedList

nodes.label: graph
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines graph as: A set of items connected by edges . Each item is called a vertex or node . Formally, a graph is a set of vertices and a binary relation between vertices, adjacency. Formal Definition: A graph G can be defined as a pair (V,E), where V is a set of vertices, and E is a set of edges between the vertices E ⊆ {(u,v) | u, v ∈ V}. If the graph is undirected, the adjacency relation defined by the edges is symmetric , or E ⊆ {{u,v} | u, v ∈ V} (sets of vertices rather than ordered pairs). If the graph does not allow self-loops , adjacency is irreflexive .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: graph

nodes.label: Dijkstra's algorithm
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Dijkstra's algorithm as: An algorithm to find the shortest paths from a single source vertex to all other vertices in a weighted, directed graph . All weights must be nonnegative.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: dijkstraalgo

nodes.label: Bellman-Ford algorithm
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Bellman-Ford algorithm as: An efficient algorithm to solve the single-source shortest-path problem . Weights may be negative. The algorithm initializes the distance to the source vertex to 0 and all other vertices to ∞. It then does V-1 passes (V is the number of vertices) over all edges relaxing, or updating, the distance to the destination of each edge. Finally it checks each edge again to detect negative weight cycles , in which case it returns false. The time complexity is O(VE) , where E is the number of edges. Also known as Ford-Bellman.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bellmanford

nodes.label: topological sort
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines topological sort as: To arrange items when some pairs of items have no comparison, that is, according to a partial order .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: topologicalSort

nodes.label: minimum spanning tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines minimum spanning tree as: A minimum-weight tree in a weighted graph which contains all of the graph's vertices . Also known as MST, shortest spanning tree, SST.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: minimumSpanningTree

nodes.label: Prim-Jarnik algorithm
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Prim-Jarnik algorithm as: Compute a minimum spanning tree by beginning with any vertex as the current tree . At each step add a least edge between any vertex not in the tree and any vertex in the tree. Continue until all vertices have been added.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: primJarnik

nodes.label: divide and conquer
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines divide and conquer as: Solve a problem, either directly because solving that instance is easy (typically, because the instance is small) or by dividing it into two or more smaller instances. Each of these smaller instances is recursively solved, and the solutions are combined to produce a solution for the original instance.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: divideAndConquer

nodes.label: backtracking
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines backtracking as: Find a solution by trying one of several choices. If the choice proves incorrect, computation backtracks or restarts at the point of choice and tries another choice. It is often convenient to maintain choice points and alternate choices using recursion .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: backtrack

nodes.label: trie
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines trie as: A tree for storing strings in which there is one node for every common prefix . The strings are stored in extra leaf nodes.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: trie

nodes.label: B-tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines B-tree as: A balanced search tree in which every node has between ⌈ m/2⌉ and m children , where m>1 is a fixed integer. m is the order . The root may have as few as 2 children. This is a good structure if much of the tree is in slow memory (disk), since the height , and hence the number of accesses, can be kept small, say one or two, by picking a large m. Also known as balanced multiway tree.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: btree

nodes.label: finite state machine
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines finite state machine as: A model of computation consisting of a set of states , a start state , an input alphabet , and a transition function that maps input symbols and current states to a next state . Computation begins in the start state with an input string. It changes to new states depending on the transition function. There are many variants, for instance, machines having actions (outputs) associated with transitions ( Mealy machine ) or states ( Moore machine ), multiple start states, transitions conditioned on no input symbol (a null) or more than one transition for a given symbol and state ( nondeterministic finite state machine ), one or more states designated as accepting states ( recognizer ), etc. Also known as finite state automaton.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: finiteStateMachine

nodes.label: balanced binary tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines balanced binary tree as: A binary tree where no leaf is more than a certain amount farther from the root than any other. After inserting or deleting a node , the tree may rebalanced with rotations .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: balancedbitr

nodes.label: priority queue
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines priority queue as: An abstract data type to efficiently support finding the item with the highest priority across a series of operations. The basic operations are: insert, find-minimum (or maximum), and delete-minimum (or maximum). Some implementations also efficiently support join two priority queues ( meld ), delete an arbitrary item, and increase the priority of a item (decrease-key). Formal Definition: The operations new(), insert(v, PQ), find-minimum or min(PQ), and delete-minimum or dm(PQ) may be defined with axiomatic semantics as follows. new() returns a priority queue min(insert(v, new())) = v dm(insert(v, new())) = new() min(insert(v, insert(w, PQ))) = if priority(v) < priority(min(insert(w, PQ))) then v else min(insert(w, PQ)) dm(insert(v, insert(w, PQ))) = if priority(v) < priority(min(insert(w, PQ))) then insert(w, PQ) else insert(v, dm(insert(w, PQ))) where PQ is a priority queue, v and w are items, and priority(v) is the priority of item v.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: priorityque

nodes.label: hash table
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines hash table as: A dictionary in which keys are mapped to array positions by hash functions . Having the keys of more than one item map to the same position is called a collision . There are many collision resolution schemes , but they may be divided into open addressing , chaining , and keeping one special overflow area. Perfect hashing avoids collisions, but may be time-consuming to create. Also known as scatter storage.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: hashtab

nodes.label: breadth-first search
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines breadth-first search as: Any search algorithm that considers neighbors of a vertex , that is, outgoing edges of the vertex's predecessor in the search, before any outgoing edges of the vertex. Extremes are searched last. This is typically implemented with a queue .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: breadthfirst

nodes.label: depth-first search
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines depth-first search as: (1) Any search algorithm that considers outgoing edges ( children ) of a vertex before any of the vertex's siblings , that is, outgoing edges of the vertex's predecessor in the search. Extremes are searched first. This is easily implemented with recursion . (2) An algorithm that marks all vertices in a directed graph in the order they are discovered and finished, partitioning the graph into a forest . Also known as DFS.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: depthfirst

nodes.label: Kruskal's algorithm
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Kruskal's algorithm as: An algorithm for computing a minimum spanning tree . It maintains a set of partial minimum spanning trees, and repeatedly adds the shortest edge in the graph whose vertices are in different partial minimum spanning trees.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: kruskalsalgo

nodes.label: dynamic programming
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines dynamic programming as: Solve an optimization problem by caching subproblem solutions ( memoization ) rather than recomputing them.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: dynamicprog

nodes.label: greedy algorithm
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines greedy algorithm as: An algorithm that always takes the best immediate, or local, solution while finding an answer. Greedy algorithms find the overall, or globally, optimal solution for some optimization problems , but may find less-than-optimal solutions for some instances of other problems.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: greedyalgo

nodes.label: binary tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines binary tree as: A tree with at most two children for each node . Formal Definition: A binary tree either is empty (no nodes), or has a root node, a left binary tree, and a right binary tree. Also known as dyadic tree.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: binarytree

nodes.label: directed graph
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines directed graph as: A graph whose edges are ordered pairs of vertices . That is, each edge can be followed from one vertex to another vertex. Formal Definition: A graph G is a pair (V,E), where V is a set of vertices, and E is a set of edges between the vertices E ⊆ {(u,v) | u, v ∈ V}. If the graph does not allow self-loops , adjacency is irreflexive , that is E ⊆ {(u,v) | u, v ∈ V ∧ u ≠ v}. Also known as digraph, oriented graph.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: directedGraph

nodes.label: deterministic finite state machine
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines deterministic finite state machine as: A finite state machine with at most one transition for each symbol and state . Also known as DFA, deterministic finite automaton.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: determFinitStateMach

nodes.label: nondeterministic finite state machine
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines nondeterministic finite state machine as: A finite state machine whose transition function maps inputs symbols and states to a (possibly empty) set of next states . The transition function also may map the null symbol (no input symbol needed) and states to next states. Also known as NFA, nondeterministic finite automaton.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: nondetermFiniteStateMach

nodes.label: array
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines array as: An assemblage of items that are randomly accessible by integers, the index. Formal Definition: Ignoring size an array may be seen as an abstract data type with the operations new(), set(i, v, A), and get(i, A), where i is a numeric index, v is a value, and A is an array. The operations may be defined with axiomatic semantics as follows. new() returns an array get(i, set(i, v, A)) = v get(i, set(j, v, A)) = get(i, A) if i ≠ j Compare this with a dictionary using integers as keys. If the contents of a new array are set to some implicit initial value v i , we could add the following rule for get. get(i, new()) = v i Typically arrays have a fixed size and use either 0-based indexing or 1-based indexing . Fixed initial size and 0-based indexing may incorporated as follows. new(s) returns an array, which has a size s size(new(s)) = s size(set(i, v, A)) = size(A) get(i, set(i, v, A)) = v if 0 ≤ i < size(A) get(i, set(j, v, A)) = get(i, A) if i ≠ j One-based or other indexing may be defined similarly.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: array

nodes.label: list
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines list as: A collection of items accessible one after another beginning at the head and ending at the tail .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: list

nodes.label: set
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines set as: An unordered collection of values where each value occurs at most once. A group of elements with three properties: (1) all elements belong to a universe , (2) either each element is a member of the set or it is not, and (3) the elements are unordered. Formal Definition: As an abstract data type , a set has a single query function, isIn(v, S), which tells whether an element is a member of the set or not, and two modifier functions, add(v, S) and remove(v, S). These may be defined with axiomatic semantics as follows. new() returns a set isIn(v, new()) = false isIn(v, add(v, S)) = true isIn(v, add(u, S)) = isIn(v , S) if v ≠ u remove(v, new()) = new() remove(v, add(v, S)) = remove(v, S) remove(v, add(u, S)) = add(u, remove(v, S)) if v ≠ u where S is a set and u and v are elements. The predicate isEmpty(S) may be defined with the following additional axioms. isEmpty(new()) = true isEmpty(add(v, S)) = false

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: set

nodes.label: tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines tree as: (1) A data structure accessed beginning at the root node. Each node is either a leaf or an internal node . An internal node has one or more child nodes and is called the parent of its child nodes. All children of the same node are siblings . Contrary to a physical tree, the root is usually depicted at the top of the structure, and the leaves are depicted at the bottom. (2) A connected , undirected , acyclic graph . It is rooted and ordered unless otherwise specified. Thanks to Joshua O'Madadhain ( [email protected] ) for the figure, 6 October 2005. Formal Definition: (1) A tree is either empty (no nodes), or a root and zero or more subtrees. The subtrees are ordered.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: tree

nodes.label: root
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines root as: The distinguished initial or fundamental item of a tree . The only item which has no parent . See the figure at tree .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: root

nodes.label: leaf
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines leaf as: A node in a tree without any children . See the figure at tree . Also known as external node, terminal node.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: leaf

nodes.label: edge
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines edge as: A connection between two vertices of a graph . In a weighted graph , each edge has an number, called a "weight". In a directed graph , an edge goes from one vertex, the source , to another, the target , and hence makes connection in only one direction. Also known as arc.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: edge

nodes.label: vertex
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines vertex as: An item in a graph . Sometimes referred to as a node .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: vertex

nodes.label: path
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines path as: A list of vertices of a graph where each vertex has an edge between it and the next vertex.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: path

nodes.label: cycle
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines cycle as: A path that starts and ends at the same vertex and includes at least one edge .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: cycle

nodes.label: weighted graph
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines weighted graph as: A graph having a weight, or number, associated with each edge . Some algorithms require all weights to be nonnegative, integral, positive, etc. Also known as edge-weighted graph.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: weightedGraph

nodes.label: connected graph
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines connected graph as: An undirected graph that has a path between every pair of vertices .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: connectedGraph

nodes.label: complete graph
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines complete graph as: An undirected graph with an edge between every pair of vertices .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: completeGraph

nodes.label: bipartite graph
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines bipartite graph as: An undirected graph where vertices can be partition ed into two sets such that no edge connects vertices in the same set.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bipartgraph

nodes.label: directed acyclic graph
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines directed acyclic graph as: A directed graph with no path that starts and ends at the same vertex . Also known as DAG, acyclic directed graph, oriented acyclic graph.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: directAcycGraph

nodes.label: abstract data type
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines abstract data type as: A set of data values and associated operations that are precisely specified independent of any particular implementation. Also known as ADT.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: abstractDataType

nodes.label: circular list
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines circular list as: A variant of a linked list in which the nominal tail is linked to the head . The entire list may be accessed starting at any item and following links until one comes to the starting item again.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: circularlist

nodes.label: circular queue
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines circular queue as: An implementation of a bounded queue using an array .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: circularQueue

nodes.label: deque
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines deque as: A data structure in which items may be added to or deleted from the head or the tail . Also known as doubly-ended queue.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: deque

nodes.label: binary heap
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines binary heap as: A complete binary tree where every node has a key more extreme (greater or less) than or equal to the key of its parent .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: binaryheap

nodes.label: Fibonacci heap
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Fibonacci heap as: A heap made of a forest of trees . The amortized cost of the operations create, insert a value, decrease a value, find minimum, and merge or join ( meld ) two heaps, is a constant Θ(1) . The delete operation takes O(log n) .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: fibonacciHeap

nodes.label: binomial heap
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines binomial heap as: A heap made of a forest of binomial trees with the heap property numbered k=0, 1, 2, …, n, each containing either 0 or 2 k nodes . Each tree is formed by linking two of its predecessors, by joining one at the root of the other. The operations of insert a value, decrease a value, delete a value, and merge or join ( meld ) two queues take O(log n) time. The find minimum operation is a constant Θ(1) .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: binomialheap

nodes.label: splay tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines splay tree as: A binary search tree in which operations that access nodes restructure the tree.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: splaytree

nodes.label: 2-3 tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines 2-3 tree as: A B-tree of order 3, that is, internal nodes have two or three children .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: two3tree

nodes.label: suffix tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines suffix tree as: A compact representation of a trie corresponding to the suffixes of a given string where all nodes with one child are merged with their parents .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: suffixtree

nodes.label: suffix array
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines suffix array as: An array of all starting positions of suffixes of a string arranged in lexicographical order . This allows a binary search or fast substring search.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: suffixarray

nodes.label: hash function
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines hash function as: A function that maps keys to integers, usually to get an even distribution on a smaller set of values. Also known as hash.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: hash

nodes.label: perfect hashing
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines perfect hashing as: A hash function that maps each different key to a distinct integer. Usually all possible keys must be known beforehand. A hash table that uses a perfect hash has no collisions . Formal Definition: A function f is perfect for a set of keys K iff ∀ j, k ∈ K f(j) = f(k) → j = k. Also known as optimal hashing.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: perfecthash

nodes.label: open addressing
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines open addressing as: A class of collision resolution schemes in which all items are stored within the hash table . In case of collision , other positions are computed, giving a probe sequence , and checked until an empty position is found. Some ways of computing possible new positions are less efficient because of clustering . Typically items never move once put in place, but in Robin Hood hashing , LCFS hashing , and other techniques, previously placed items may move.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: openAddressing

nodes.label: linear probing
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines linear probing as: A hash table in which a collision is resolved by putting the item in the next empty place in the array following the occupied place. Even with a moderate load factor , primary clustering tends to slow retrieval.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: linearprobng

nodes.label: double hashing
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines double hashing as: A method of open addressing for a hash table in which a collision is resolved by searching the table for an empty place at intervals given by a different hash function, thus minimizing clustering . Also known as rehashing.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: doublehashng

nodes.label: cuckoo hashing
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines cuckoo hashing as: A dictionary implemented with two hash tables , T 1 and T 2 , and two different hash functions , h 1 and h 2 . Each key , k, is either in T 1 [h 1 (k)] or T 2 [h 2 (k)]. A new key , k, is stored in T 1 [h 1 (k)]. If that location is already occupied by another key, l, the other key is moved to T 2 [h 2 (l)]. Keys are moved back and forth until a key moves to an empty location or a limit is reached. If the limit is reached, new hash functions are chosen, and the tables are rehashed. For tables that are a bit less than half full and with carefully chosen universal hashing functions, performance is good. A key is deleted by removing it from a table.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: cuckooHashing

nodes.label: recursion
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines recursion as: An algorithmic technique where a function, in order to accomplish a task, calls itself with some part of the task.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: recursion

nodes.label: iteration
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines iteration as: Solve a problem by repeatedly working on successive parts of the problem.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: iteration

nodes.label: memoization
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines memoization as: Save (memoize) a computed answer for possible later reuse, rather than recomputing the answer.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: memoize

nodes.label: branch and bound
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines branch and bound as: An algorithmic technique to find the optimal solution by keeping the best solution found so far. If a partial solution cannot improve on the best, it is abandoned.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: branchNbound

nodes.label: exhaustive search
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines exhaustive search as: An algorithm that finds a solution by trying every possibility.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: exhaustiveSearch

nodes.label: interpolation search
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines interpolation search as: Search a sorted array by estimating the next position to check based on a linear interpolation of the search key and the values at the ends of the search interval. Also known as extrapolation search.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: interpolationSearch

nodes.label: jump search
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines jump search as: Search a sorted array by checking every j th item until the right area is found, then doing a linear search . The optimum for n items is when j=√ n. Also known as block search.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: jumpsearch

nodes.label: Fibonaccian search
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Fibonaccian search as: Search a sorted array by narrowing possible locations to progressively smaller intervals. Begin with two Fibonacci numbers , p (F(n)) and q (F(n+1)), such that p < n ≤ q, where n is the size of the array. The first step checks location p. The size of the next interval is p, if the key is less than the item at that location, or q-p (F(n-1)) if it is greater.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: fibonaccianSearch

nodes.label: all pairs shortest path
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines all pairs shortest path as: Find the weight (or length) of the shortest paths between all pairs of vertices in a weighted, directed graph .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: allPairsShortestPath

nodes.label: transitive closure
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines transitive closure as: An extension or superset of a binary relation such that whenever (a,b) and (b,c) are in the extension, (a,c) is also in the extension.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: transitiveClosure

nodes.label: Euclid's algorithm
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Euclid's algorithm as: An algorithm to compute the greatest common divisor of two positive integers. It is Euclid(a,b){if (b=0) then return a; else return Euclid(b, a mod b);} . The run time complexity is O((log a)(log b)) bit operations. Also known as Euclidean algorithm.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: euclidalgo

nodes.label: fast fourier transform
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines fast fourier transform as: An algorithm to convert a set of uniformly spaced points from the time domain to the frequency domain. Also known as FFT.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: fastFourierTransform

nodes.label: Huffman coding
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Huffman coding as: A minimal variable-length character coding based on the frequency of each character. First, each character becomes a one-node binary tree , with the character as the only node . The character's frequency is the tree's frequency. Two trees with the least frequencies are joined as the subtrees of a new root that is assigned the sum of their frequencies. Repeat until all characters are in one tree. One code bit represents each level . Thus more frequent characters are near the root and are coded with few bits, and rare characters are far from the root and are coded with many bits. Also known as static Huffman coding.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: huffmanCoding

nodes.label: arithmetic coding
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines arithmetic coding as: A minimal variable-length message coding based on the frequency of each character. The message is represented by a fraction which is the repeated offset-plus-product reduction of the range (offset) and probability (product) of each character.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: arithmeticCoding

nodes.label: Lempel-Ziv-Welch
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Lempel-Ziv-Welch as: A compression algorithm that codes strings of characters with codes of a fixed number of bits. Every new string in the input is added to a table until it is full. The codes of existing strings are output instead of the strings. Also known as LZW compression.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: lempelZivWelch

nodes.label: string matching
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines string matching as: The problem of finding occurrence(s) of a pattern string within another string or body of text. There are many different algorithms for efficient searching. Also known as exact string matching, string searching, text searching.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: stringMatching

nodes.label: Boyer-Moore
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Boyer-Moore as: A string matching algorithm that compares characters from the end of the pattern to its beginning. When characters don't match, searching jumps to the next possible match: the farthest of a table like that used in the Knuth-Morris-Pratt algorithm and the next matching position in the pattern .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: boyermoore

nodes.label: Shell sort
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Shell sort as: The first diminishing increment sort . On each pass i sets of n/i items are sorted, typically with insertion sort . On each succeeding pass, i is reduced until it is 1 for the last pass. A good series of i values is important to efficiency.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: shellsort

nodes.label: comb sort
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines comb sort as: An in-place sort algorithm that repeatedly reorders different pairs of items. On each pass swap pairs of items separated by the increment or gap, if needed, and reduce the gap (divide it by about 1.3). The gap starts at about 3/4 of the number of items. Continue until the gap is 1 and a pass had no swaps.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: combSort

nodes.label: gnome sort
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines gnome sort as: Put items in order by comparing the current item with the previous item. If they are in order, move to the next item (or stop if the end is reached). If they are out of order, swap them and move to the previous item. If there is no previous item, move to the next item.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: gnomeSort

nodes.label: in-place sort
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines in-place sort as: A sort algorithm in which the sorted items occupy the same storage as the original ones. These algorithms may use o(n) additional memory for bookkeeping, but at most a constant number of items are kept in auxiliary memory at any time. Also known as sort in place.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: inplacesort

nodes.label: comparison sort
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines comparison sort as: Any sort algorithm using comparisons between keys , and nothing else about the keys, to arrange items in a predetermined order. An alternative is a restricted universe sort such as counting sort or bucket sort .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: comparisnsrt

nodes.label: external sort
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines external sort as: Any sort algorithm that uses external memory, such as tape or disk, during the sort. Since most common sort algorithms assume high-speed random access to all intermediate memory, they are unsuitable if the values to be sorted don't fit in main memory.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: externalsort

nodes.label: internal sort
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines internal sort as: Any sort algorithm which uses exclusively main memory during the sort. This assumes high-speed random access to all memory.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: internalsort

nodes.label: bitonic sort
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines bitonic sort as: Compare, and swap if necessary, pairs of elements in parallel. Subsets are sorted then merged. Also known as Batcher sort.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bitonicSort

nodes.label: finite state transducer
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines finite state transducer as: A finite state machine specifically with a read-only input and a write-only output. The input and output cannot be reread or changed.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: finiteStateTransducer

nodes.label: Turing machine
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Turing machine as: A model of computation consisting of a finite state machine controller, a read-write head, and an unbounded sequential tape. Depending on the current state and symbol read on the tape, the machine can change its state and move the head to the left or right. Unless otherwise specified, a Turing machine is deterministic .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: turingMachine

nodes.label: nondeterministic Turing machine
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines nondeterministic Turing machine as: A Turing machine which has more than one next state for some combinations of contents of the current cell and current state. An input is accepted if any move sequence leads to acceptance.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: nondetermTuringMach

nodes.label: big-O notation
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines big-O notation as: A theoretical measure of the execution of an algorithm , usually the time or memory needed, given the problem size n, which is usually the number of items. Informally, saying some equation f(n) = O(g(n)) means it is less than some constant multiple of g(n). The notation is read, "f of n is big oh of g of n". Formal Definition: f(n) = O(g(n)) means there are positive constants c and k, such that 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ cg(n) for all n ≥ k. The values of c and k must be fixed for the function f and must not depend on n. Also known as O, asymptotic upper bound.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bigOnotation

nodes.label: asymptotic bound
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines asymptotic bound as: A curve representing the limit of a function. That is, the distance between a function and the curve tends to zero. The function may or may not intersect the bounding curve.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: asymptoticBound

nodes.label: NP-complete
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines NP-complete as: The complexity class of decision problems for which answers can be checked for correctness, given a certificate , by an algorithm whose run time is polynomial in the size of the input (that is, it is NP ) and no other NP problem is more than a polynomial factor harder. Informally, a problem is NP-complete if answers can be verified quickly, and a quick algorithm to solve this problem can be used to solve all other NP problems quickly.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: npcomplete

nodes.label: polynomial time
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines polynomial time as: When the execution time of a computation, m(n), is no more than a polynomial function of the problem size, n. More formally m(n) = O(n k ) where k is a constant.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: polynomialtm

nodes.label: D-tree

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: DTree

nodes.label: Dutch national flag
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Dutch national flag as: Rearrange elements in an array into three groups: bottom, middle, and top. One algorithm is to have the top group grow down from the top of the array, the bottom group grow up from the bottom, and keep the middle group just above the bottom. The algorithm stores the locations just below the top group, just above the bottom, and just above the middle in three indexes. At each step, examine the element just above the middle. If it belongs to the top group, swap it with the element just below the top. If it belongs in the bottom, swap it with the element just above the bottom. If it is in the middle, leave it. Update the appropriate index. Complexity is Θ(n) moves and examinations.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: DutchNationalFlag

nodes.label: Euler's formula
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Euler's formula as: For convex polyhedron, V - E + F = 2, where V is the number of vertices, E is the number of edges, and F is the number of faces.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: EulersFormula

nodes.label: JSort

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: JSort

nodes.label: LCS
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines LCS as: Either longest common subsequence or longest common substring .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: LCS

nodes.label: Levenshtein distance
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Levenshtein distance as: (1) The smallest number of insertions, deletions, and substitutions required to change one string or tree into another. (2) A Θ(m × n) algorithm to compute the distance between strings, where m and n are the lengths of the strings. Also known as edit distance.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: Levenshtein

nodes.label: Merkle tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Merkle tree as: A tree (usually a binary tree ) in which each internal node has a hash of all the information in the leaf nodes under it. Specifically, each internal node has a hash of the information in its children . Each leaf has a hash of the block of information it represents. All leaf nodes are at the same depth . All nodes are as far left as possible. To add a block (leaf) to a full tree, a new root is created with the old root as its left child. Its right child is a degenerate tree (only left subtrees) all the way to the leaf level. Also known as hash tree.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: MerkleTree

nodes.label: SSTable
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines SSTable as: An immutable dictionary stored on disk. Values are far larger than keys. Keys and values are in key-order in a "data block". Ordered keys are in an "index block", where each key has an offset into its location in the data block. Also known as sorted-string table.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: SSTable

nodes.label: absolute performance guarantee
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines absolute performance guarantee as: An approximation algorithm will return a solution at most a bounded amount more (or less, as appropriate) than the optimum.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: absolute

nodes.label: (a,b)-tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines (a,b)-tree as: A search tree with the restrictions that all leaves are at the same depth and all internal nodes have between a and b children , where a and b are integers such that 2 ≤ a ≤ (b+1)/2. The root may have as few as 2 children.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: abtree

nodes.label: accepting state

nodes.label: Ackermann's function

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: ackermann

nodes.label: adaptive heap sort

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: adaptiveHeapSort

nodes.label: adaptive Huffman coding
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines adaptive Huffman coding as: A near-minimal variable-length character coding that changes based on the frequency of characters processed. As characters are processed, frequencies are updated and codes are changed (or, the coding tree is modified). Also known as dynamic Huffman coding.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: adaptiveHuffman

nodes.label: adaptive sort
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines adaptive sort as: A sorting algorithm that can take advantage of existing order in the input, reducing its requirements for computational resources as a function of the disorder in the input.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: adaptivesort

nodes.label: adaptive k-d tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines adaptive k-d tree as: A tree for multidimensional points where successive levels may be split along different dimensions.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: adaptkdtree

nodes.label: address-calculation sort

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: addresscalc

nodes.label: adjacency-list representation

An undirected graph may be represented by having vertex j in the list for vertex i and vertex i in the list for vertex j.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: adjacencyListRep

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: adversary

nodes.label: Aho-Corasick

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: ahoCorasick

nodes.label: algorithm FGK

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: algorithmFGK

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: allSimplePaths

nodes.label: alphabet

nodes.label: American flag sort
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines American flag sort as: An efficient, in-place variant of radix sort that distributes items into hundreds of buckets . The first step counts the number of items in each bucket, and the second step computes where each bucket will start in the array. The last step cyclically permutes items to their proper bucket. Since the buckets are in order in the array, there is no collection step. The name comes by analogy with the Dutch national flag problem in the last step: efficiently partition the array into many "stripes". Using some efficiency techniques, it is twice as fast as quicksort for large sets of strings.

nodes.label: bag
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines bag as: An unordered collection of values that may have duplicates. Formal Definition: A bag has a single query function, numberIn(v, B), which tells how many copies of an element are in the bag, and two modifier functions, add(v, B) and remove(v, B). These may be defined with axiomatic semantics as follows. new() returns a bag numberIn(v, new()) = 0 numberIn(v, add(v, B)) = 1 + numberIn(v, B) numberIn(v, add(u, B)) = numberIn(v, B) if v ≠ u remove(v, new()) = new() remove(v, add(v, B)) = B remove(v, add(u, B)) = add(u, remove(v, B)) if v ≠ u where B is a bag and u and v are elements. The predicate isEmpty(B) may be defined with the following additional axioms. isEmpty(new()) = true isEmpty(add(v, B)) = false Also known as multi-set.

It then repeatedly merges the two streams and puts each merged run into one of two output streams until there is a single sorted output.

Formal Definition: The operations new to this variant of stack, branch(S, T) and notch(v), may be defined with axiomatic semantics as follows. top(branch(S, T)) = top(S) notch(new()) = false notch(push(v, S)) = false notch(branch(S, T)) = true Also known as saguaro stack.

nodes.label: dictionary

Formal Definition: The operations new(), insert(k, v, D), and find(k, D) may be defined with axiomatic semantics as follows. new() returns a dictionary find(k, insert(k, v, D)) = v find(k, insert(j, v, D)) = find(k, D) if k ≠ j where k and j are keys, v is a value, and D is a dictionary. The modifier function delete(k, D) may be defined as follows. delete(k, new()) = new() delete(k, insert(k, v, D)) = delete(k, D) delete(k, insert(j, v, D)) = insert(j, v, delete(k, D)) if k ≠ j If we want find to be a total function , we could define find(k, new()) using a special value: fail . This only changes the return type of find. find(k, new()) = fail Also known as association list, map, property list.

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines dynamization transformation as: A data structuring technique that can make a static data structure dynamic . In so doing, the performance of the dynamic structure will exhibit certain space-time tradeoffs.

nodes.label: easy split, hard merge

nodes.label: edge connectivity

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines edge crossing as: Two different edges cross in a graph drawing if their geometric representations intersect. The number of crossings in a graph drawing is the number of pairs of edges which cross.

nodes.label: edit operation
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines edit operation as: On a string , the operation of deletion, insertion, or substitution performed on a single symbol. On a tree , the deletion of a node v followed by the reassignment of all children of v to the node of which v was formerly a child , the insertion of a new node followed by the reassignment of some arcs departing from the parent of the new node, or the substitution of the label of one of the nodes with another label. Each edit operation may have an associated nonnegative real number representing its cost.

nodes.label: efficiency
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines efficiency as: The resources an algorithm used to find an answer. It is usually measured in terms of the theoretical computations, such as comparisons or data moves, the memory used, the number of messages passed, the number of disk accesses, etc.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: efficiency

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines elastic-bucket trie as: A variant of a bucket trie in which each leaf node for n strings is a bucket allocated to hold exactly n strings.

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines element uniqueness as: The problem of determining if there are duplicates in a set of numbers.

nodes.label: Euclidean traveling salesman problem
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Euclidean traveling salesman problem as: Find a path of minimum Euclidean distance between points in a plane which includes each point exactly once and returns to its starting point.

nodes.label: Euler cycle
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Euler cycle as: A path through a graph which starts and ends at the same vertex and includes every edge exactly once. Also known as Eulerian path, Königsberg bridges problem.

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Eulerian graph as: A graph that has an Euler cycle .

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines exclusive read, concurrent write as: A parallel memory model in which only one processor can read from any one memory location at one time, but multiple processors can write simultaneously to a single memory location. Also known as ERCW.

nodes.label: exclusive read, exclusive write
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines exclusive read, exclusive write as: A parallel memory model in which only one processor can read from any one memory location at one time, and only one processor can write to any one memory location at one time. Also known as EREW.

nodes.label: existential state
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines existential state as: A state in a nondeterministic Turing machine from which the machine accepts if any move leads to acceptance.

nodes.label: extended Euclid's algorithm
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines extended Euclid's algorithm as: An algorithm to find the greatest common divisor , g , of two positive integers, a and b , and coefficients, h and j , such that g = ha + jb .

nodes.label: extended binary tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines extended binary tree as: A binary tree with special nodes replacing every null subtree. Every regular node has two children , and every special node has no children.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: extendedBinaryTree

nodes.label: extendible hashing
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines extendible hashing as: A hash table in which the hash function is the last few bits of the key and the table refers to buckets . Table entries with the same final bits may use the same bucket. If a bucket overflows, it splits, and if only one entry referred to it, the table doubles in size. If a bucket is emptied by deletion, entries using it are changed to refer to an adjoining bucket, and the table may be halved.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: extendibleHashing

nodes.label: extended k-d tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines extended k-d tree as: A spatial access method where successive levels are split along different dimensions into nonoverlapping cells. Objects are indexed in all cells they intersect.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: extendkdtree

nodes.label: external memory algorithm
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines external memory algorithm as: An algorithm that is efficient when accessing most of the data is very slow, such as, on disk.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: externalMemoryAlgo

nodes.label: external memory data structure
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines external memory data structure as: A data structure that is efficient even when accessing most of the data is very slow, such as, on a disk.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: externalMemoryDataStr

nodes.label: external quicksort
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines external quicksort as: Read the M/2 first and last elements into a buffer (the buffer acts like the pivot in quicksort ), and sort them. Read the next element from the beginning or end to balance writing. If the next element is less than the least of the buffer, write it to available space at the beginning. If greater than the greatest, write it to the end. Otherwise write the greatest or least of the buffer, and put the next element in the buffer. Keep the maximum lower and minimum upper keys written to avoid resorting middle elements that are in order. When done, write the buffer. Recursively sort the smaller partition, and loop to sort the remaining partition.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: externalQuicksort

nodes.label: external index
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines external index as: An auxiliary data structure added to a main data structure to improve operations, such as a search on a secondary key .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: externalindx

nodes.label: external merge
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines external merge as: To combine multiple sorted data streams into a single sorted stream using external storage.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: externalmerg

nodes.label: extremal
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines extremal as: Some of the entries of the auxiliary array used in a string matching algorithm. An entry is d-extremal if it is the deepest entry on its diagonal to be given value d.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: extremal

nodes.label: extreme point
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines extreme point as: A corner point of a polyhedron . More formally, a point which cannot be expressed as a convex combination of other points in the polyhedron.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: extremepoint

nodes.label: facility location
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines facility location as: Given a set of demand points, a distance function, and a parameter p, find a set of p supply objects (points, lines, segments, etc.) which minimizes some distance objective function . The function may be the maximum distance between any demand point and the nearest supply, so no demand point is too far from a supply, or the sum of distances to the nearest supply.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: facilityloc

nodes.label: fathoming

nodes.label: Fibonacci tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Fibonacci tree as: A variant of a binary tree where a tree of order n (n>1) has a left subtree of order n-1 and a right subtree of order n-2. An order 0 Fibonacci tree has no nodes , and an order 1 tree has 1 node.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: fibonacciTree

nodes.label: Find
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Find as: An algorithm to select the k th smallest element of an array and partition the array around it. First, partition around the value of the k th element. If the split is not at element k, move the upper or lower boundary and partition again.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: find

nodes.label: finitary tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines finitary tree as: A tree with a finite number of children at every node .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: finitarytree

nodes.label: flow

nodes.label: flow conservation
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines flow conservation as: The property that no vertex , except the source and sink , of a flow network creates or stores flow. More formally, the incoming flow is the same as the outgoing flow, or, the net flow is 0.

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Ford-Fulkerson method as: Given a flow function and its corresponding residual graph (a maximum-flow problem ), select a path from the source to the sink along which the flow can be increased and increase the flow. Repeat until there are no such paths.

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines fractional knapsack problem as: Given materials of different values per unit volume and maximum amounts, find the most valuable mix of materials which fit in a knapsack of fixed volume. nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines hard split, easy merge as: A recursive algorithm, especially a sort algorithm, where dividing (splitting) into smaller problems is time consuming or complex and combining (merging) the solutions is quick or trivial.

nodes.label: head

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines horizontal visibility map as: A partition of the plane into regions by drawing a horizontal straight line through each vertex p of a planar straight-line graph until it intersects an edge e of the graph or extends to infinity. The edge e is said to be horizontally visible from p.

nodes.label: hsadelta
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines hsadelta as: An algorithm to produce a sequence of insert and copy commands (an edit script ) which creates a new version file from a reference file. To begin, hash every block of the reference file and store every hash in a hash value array . Build a suffix array and three other data structures for quick access. Beginning at the first location in the version file, hash a block and look for the longest match in the reference file. Upon a match, encode an insert back to the previous match and a copy of the match. If no match, look at the next location. At the end, encode an insert for remaining unmatched characters.

nodes.label: ideal random shuffle

nodes.label: ideal merge
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines ideal merge as: Merge n sorted streams into one output stream. To begin the streams are sorted by the value of the head element of each. Then the head of the first stream, which is the least since the streams were sorted, is removed and written to the output. That stream is inserted back into the list of streams according to its new head. Taking the head of the first stream and reinserting that stream is repeated until all elements have been processed. Using linear search to insert a stream into the list, the execution time is Θ(M N) where M is the total number of elements. Keeping the streams in a heap , the execution time is Θ(M log N) .

nodes.label: intersection

nodes.label: inverse suffix array

nodes.label: inversion list
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines inversion list as: A set of non-overlapping numeric ranges, stored in an array in increasing order. Items in odd indexes begin ranges, and items in even indexes are the first number after the ends. Use a form of binary search to determine if a number is in any of the ranges. If the search ends on an odd index (a beginning), the number is in the set. If the search ends on an even index (a just-after-end) or outside the array, it is not in the set.

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines inverted index as: An index into a set of texts of the words in the texts. The index is accessed by some search method. Each index entry gives the word and a list of texts, possibly with locations within the text, where the word occurs.

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines invertible Bloom lookup table as: Algorithms and an array of cells to store key/value pairs. Each cell has a count of how many pairs are mapped to the cell, the sum of the keys mapped to it, and the sum of the values mapped to it. Using k hash functions , each pair is mapped to T[h 1 (k)], T[h 2 (k)], ..., T[h k (k)]. Also known as IBLT.

nodes.label: isomorphic

nodes.label: J sort

nodes.label: Jaro-Winkler
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Jaro-Winkler as: A measure of similarity between two strings . The Jaro measure is the weighted sum of percentage of matched characters from each file and transposed characters. Winkler increased this measure for matching initial characters, then rescaled it by a piecewise function, whose intervals and weights depend on the type of string (first name, last name, street, etc.).

nodes.label: jelly-fish
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines jelly-fish as: A theoretical data structure for n items. It starts with a balanced binary search tree of about √(n) nodes. The leaf nodes lead to "tentacles" or linked lists , each of about √(n) nodes.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: jellyfish

nodes.label: Johnson-Trotter
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Johnson-Trotter as: Generate permutations by swapping one adjacent pair of elements at a time. Also known as Steinhaus-Johnson-Trotter, Trotter-Johnson.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: johnsonTrotter

nodes.label: Johnson's algorithm
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Johnson's algorithm as: An algorithm to solve the all pairs shortest path problem in a sparse weighted, directed graph . First, it adds a new node with zero weight edges from it to all other nodes, and runs the Bellman-Ford algorithm to check for negative weight cycles and find h(v), the least weight of a path from the new node to node v. Next it reweights the edges using the nodes' h(v) values. Finally for each node, it runs Dijkstra's algorithm and stores the computed least weight to other nodes, reweighted using the nodes' h(v) values, as the final weight. The time complexity is O(V²log V + VE) .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: johnsonsAlgorithm

nodes.label: k²-tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines k²-tree as: A compact representation of a sparse directed graph . It requires 1 to 3 bits per edge. sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: k2tree

nodes.label: Karnaugh map
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Karnaugh map as: A method for minimizing a boolean expression , usually aided by a rectangular map of the value of the expression for all possible input values. Input values are arranged in a Gray code . Maximal rectangular groups that cover the inputs where the expression is true give a minimum implementation. Also known as Veitch diagram, KV diagram.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: karnaughmap

nodes.label: Karp-Rabin
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Karp-Rabin as: A string matching algorithm that compares string's hash values, rather than the strings themselves. For efficiency, the hash value of the next position in the text is easily computed from the hash value of the current position. Also known as Rabin-Karp.

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines K-dominant match as: A match [i,j] having rank k and such that for any other pair [i',j'] of rank k either i'>i and j'≤ j or i' ≤ i and j'>j.

nodes.label: Knuth-Morris-Pratt algorithm
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Knuth-Morris-Pratt algorithm as: A string matching algorithm that turns the search string into a finite state machine , then runs the machine with the string to be searched as the input string. Execution time is O(m+n) , where m is the length of the search string, and n is the length of the string to be searched. Also known as KMP.

nodes.label: Kolmogorov complexity
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Kolmogorov complexity as: The minimum number of bits into which a string can be compressed without losing information. This is defined with respect to a fixed, but universal decompression scheme, given by a universal Turing machine .

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines k-way merge sort as: A merge sort that sorts a data stream using repeated merges. It distributes the input into k streams by repeatedly reading a block of input that fits in memory, called a run , sorting it, then writing it to the next stream. It merges runs from the k streams into an output stream. It then repeatedly distributes the runs in the output stream to the k streams and merges them until there is a single sorted output. Also known as p-way merge sort.

nodes.label: k-way merge
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines k-way merge as: Combine k sorted data streams into a single sorted stream.

nodes.label: little-o notation
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines little-o notation as: A theoretical measure of the execution of an algorithm , usually the time or memory needed, given the problem size n, which is usually the number of items. Informally, saying some equation f(n) = o(g(n)) means f(n) becomes insignificant relative to g(n) as n approaches infinity. The notation is read, "f of n is little oh of g of n". Formal Definition: f(n) = o(g(n)) means for all c > 0 there exists some k > 0 such that 0 ≤ f(n) < cg(n) for all n ≥ k. The value of k must not depend on n, but may depend on c.

nodes.label: locality-sensitive hashing

The hash functions come from a family of functions. Finding: look up the query point in each hash table, and compute the distance from the query point of every point in the bucket.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: localitySensitiveHashing

nodes.label: local optimum
