nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines reservoir sampling as: Randomly select k items from a stream of items of unknown length. Save the first k items in an array of size k. For each item j, j > k, choose a random integer M from 1 to j (inclusive). If M ≤ k, replace item M of the array with item j.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: reservoirSampling

nodes.label: restricted universe sort
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines restricted universe sort as: A sort algorithm that operates on the basis that the keys are members of a restricted set of values. They may not require comparisons of keys to perform the sorting.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: restricted

nodes.label: R-file
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines R-file as: A spatial access method which divides space into a hierarchically of nested boxes. Objects are indexed in the lowest cell which completely contains them.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rfile

nodes.label: ρ-approximation algorithm
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines ρ-approximation algorithm as: An approximation algorithm guaranteed to find a solution at most (or at least, as appropriate) ρ times the optimum. The ratio ρ is the performance ratio or relative performance guarantee of the algorithm.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rhoapproxmtn

nodes.label: Rice's method
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Rice's method as: A method of complex asymptotics that can handle certain alternating sums arising in the analysis of algorithms.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: ricesmethod

nodes.label: right-threaded tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines right-threaded tree as: A variant of a threaded tree in which only the right thread, i.e. link to the successor, of each node is maintained.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rightThreadedTree

nodes.label: right rotation
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines right rotation as: (1) In a binary search tree , pushing a node N down and to the right to balance the tree. N's left child replaces N, and the left child's right child becomes N's left child. (2) In an array , moving all items to the next higher location. The last item is moved to the first location, which is now vacant. (3) In a list , removing the tail and inserting it at the head . Also known as rotate right.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rightrotatn

nodes.label: Robin Hood hashing
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Robin Hood hashing as: In case of collision , the item with the longer probe sequence stays in the position. The other item is moved. This tends to equalize the length of probe sequences.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: robinHoodHashing

nodes.label: rooted tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines rooted tree as: A tree in which one node is designated as the root . Also known as oriented tree.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rootedtree

nodes.label: rotation
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines rotation as: To switch children and parents among two or three adjacent nodes to restore balance to a tree .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rotation

nodes.label: RP
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines RP as: The class of languages for which membership can be determined in polynomial time by a probabilistic Turing machine with no false acceptances and less than half false rejections. "RP" means " R andomized P olynomial" time. Formal Definition: For a language, S, there exists a probabilistic Turing machine , M, that accepts or rejects any string in polynomial time . If w ∉ S, M rejects w. If w ∈ S, M accepts w with a probability at least 1/2. Also known as randomized polynomial time.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rp

nodes.label: R-tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines R-tree as: (1) A spatial access method that splits space with hierarchically nested, and possibly overlapping, boxes. The tree is height-balanced. (2) A recursion tree .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rtree

nodes.label: run time
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines run time as: (1) The amount of time needed to execute an algorithm . (2) The time when a compiled program is executing, versus compile time.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: runtime

nodes.label: saturated edge
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines saturated edge as: An edge in a flow network which has the maximum possible flow.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: saturatedEdge

nodes.label: SBB tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines SBB tree as: A symmetric binary B-tree. Now known as a red-black tree .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: sbbtree

nodes.label: scan
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines scan as: A parallel operation in which each element in an array or linked list receives the sum of all previous elements. Also known as prefix sums.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: scan

nodes.label: scapegoat tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines scapegoat tree as: A binary search tree that needs no balance information. Search time is logarithmic , and the amortized cost of update is logarithmic .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: scapegoatTree

nodes.label: search tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines search tree as: A tree where every subtree of a node has keys less than any other subtree of the node to its right. The keys in a node are conceptually between subtrees and are greater than any keys in subtrees to its left and less than any keys in subtrees to its right.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: searchtree

nodes.label: search tree property
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines search tree property as: When the key of every node of a binary tree is larger than the key of its left child and smaller than its right child.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: searchtrprop

nodes.label: secant search
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines secant search as: Search a sorted array by estimating the next position to check based on the values at the two previous positions checked.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: secantSearch

nodes.label: secondary clustering
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines secondary clustering as: The tendency for some collision resolution schemes to create long run of filled slots away from a key hash position, e.g., along the probe sequence .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: secondaryClustering

nodes.label: segment
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines segment as: (1) The substring of a pattern delimited by two don't cares or one don't care and beginning or end of the pattern. (2) A substring .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: segment

nodes.label: Select
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Select as: A four-part algorithm to select the k th smallest element of an array . Part 1) Consider the array as groups of 5 elements; sort and find the median of each group. 2) Use Select recursively to find x , the median of the medians. 3) Next partition the array around x . 4) Let i be the number of elements in the low side of the partition. If k ≤ i, use Select recursively to find the k th element of the low side. Otherwise Select the k-i th element of the high side.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: select

nodes.label: select and partition
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines select and partition as: Given an array A of n elements and a positive integer k ≤ n, find the k th smallest element of A and partition the array such that A[1], …, A[k-1] ≤ A[k] ≤ A[k+1], …, A[n].

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: selectAndPartition

nodes.label: select mode
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines select mode as: An algorithm to find the mode, or most frequently occurring value, in a group of elements.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: selectmode

nodes.label: self-organizing list
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines self-organizing list as: A list that reorders the elements based on some self-organizing heuristic [Wikipedia] to improve average access time.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: selfOrganizingList

nodes.label: self-loop
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines self-loop as: An edge of a graph which starts and ends at the same vertex .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: selfloop

nodes.label: semidefinite programming
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines semidefinite programming as: A generalization of a linear program in which any subset of the variables may be constrained to form a semidefinite matrix.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: semidefinite

nodes.label: separate chaining
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines separate chaining as: A scheme in which each position in the hash table has a list to handle collisions . Each position may be just a link to the list ( direct chaining ) or may be an item and a link, essentially, the head of a list. In the latter, one item is in the table, and other colliding items are in the list. Also known as external chaining.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: separateChaining

nodes.label: separation theorem
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines separation theorem as: A theorem showing that two complexity classes are distinct. Most separation theorems have been proved by diagonalization .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: separatnthrm

nodes.label: set packing
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines set packing as: An optimization problem to find the largest number of mutually disjoint subsets that cover a given set of sets .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: setpacking

nodes.label: shadow heap
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines shadow heap as: A heap , implemented in an array , adjacent to an unordered table. The shadow is the table nodes and all their (recursive) parents , by array index, in the heap.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: shadowheap

nodes.label: shadow merge
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines shadow merge as: An algorithm to merge two heaps by concatenating the smaller heap to the larger, then reordering just the concatenated nodes and their parents to restore the heap property.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: shadowmerge

nodes.label: shadow merge insert
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines shadow merge insert as: An algorithm to insert a new node into a shadow heap . The new node is placed in the unordered table. When the table grows beyond some threshold size, table nodes and all their parents are reordered so everything is a heap.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: shadowmrgins

nodes.label: Shannon-Fano coding
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Shannon-Fano coding as: A variable-length coding based on the frequency of occurrence of each character. Divide the characters into two sets with the frequency of each set as close to half as possible, and assign the sets either 0 or 1 coding. Repeatedly divide the sets until each character has a unique coding.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: shannonFano

nodes.label: shared memory
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines shared memory as: All processors have the same global image of (and access to) all of the memory.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: sharedmemory

nodes.label: Shift-Or
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Shift-Or as: A string matching algorithm which keeps an array of bits, R, showing if prefixes of the pattern don't match at the current place. Before searching, mismatch arrays are computed for each character in the alphabet and saved in an array, S. For the next position, with the character c, R = shift(R) or S[c]. If the last bit of R is 0, the pattern matches.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: shiftOr

nodes.label: shortest common supersequence
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines shortest common supersequence as: Find the shortest string that contains two or more strings as subsequences .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: shortestCommonSuperseq

nodes.label: shortest common superstring
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines shortest common superstring as: Find the shortest string that contains two or more strings as substrings .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: shortestCommonSuperstring

nodes.label: shuffle sort
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines shuffle sort as: A distribution sort algorithm that begins by removing the first 1/8 of the n items, sorting them (recursively), and putting them in an array. This creates n/8 buckets to which the remaining 7/8 of the items are distributed. Each bucket is then sorted, and the buckets are concatenated.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: shuffleSort

nodes.label: sibling
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines sibling as: A node in a tree that has the same parent as another node is its sibling.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: sibling

nodes.label: sieve of Eratosthenes
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines sieve of Eratosthenes as: An algorithm to find all prime numbers up to a certain N. Begin with an (unmarked) array of integers from 2 to N. The first unmarked integer, 2, is the first prime. Mark every multiple of this prime. Repeatedly take the next unmarked integer as the next prime and mark every multiple of the prime.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: sieve

nodes.label: sift up
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines sift up as: Restoring the heap property by swapping a node with its parent , and repeating the process on the parent until the root is reached or the heap property is satisfied.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: siftup

nodes.label: signature
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines signature as: The types or domains , and order, in some representations, of inputs to and outputs from a function .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: signature

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines ∼ as: (1) Proportional to. (2) Asymptotically equal to. A theoretical measure of the execution of an algorithm , usually the time or memory needed, given the problem size n, which is usually the number of items. Informally, saying some equation f(n) ∼ g(n) means it grows at the same rate as g(n). More formally, it means lim x → ∞ f(x)/g(x) = 1.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: sim

nodes.label: simple uniform hashing
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines simple uniform hashing as: The assumption or goal that items are equally likely to hash to any value.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: simpleUniformHashing

nodes.label: simple merge
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines simple merge as: Merge n sorted streams into one output stream. All the stream heads are compared, and the head with the least key is removed and written to the output. This is repeated until all streams are empty.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: simplemerge

nodes.label: simple path
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines simple path as: A path that repeats no vertex , except that the first and last may be the same vertex.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: simplepath

nodes.label: simplex
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines simplex as: The simplest N-dimensional polytope . The generalization of a triangle (2D) or tetrahedron (3D).

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: simplex

nodes.label: simulated annealing
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines simulated annealing as: A technique to find a good solution to an optimization problem by trying random variations of the current solution. A worse variation is accepted as the new solution with a probability that decreases as the computation proceeds. The slower the cooling schedule , or rate of decrease, the more likely the algorithm is to find an optimal or near- optimal solution .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: simulatedAnnealing

nodes.label: simulation theorem
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines simulation theorem as: One kind of computation can be simulated by another kind within stated complexity bounds. Most known containment or equality relationships between complexity classes were proved this way.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: simulatnthrm

nodes.label: single-destination shortest-path problem
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines single-destination shortest-path problem as: Find the shortest path from each vertex in a weighted, directed graph to a specific destination vertex.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: singleDestShortestPath

nodes.label: single-source shortest-path problem
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines single-source shortest-path problem as: Find the shortest paths from a specific source vertex to every other vertex in a weighted, directed graph . Dijkstra's algorithm solves this if all weights are nonnegative. The Bellman-Ford algorithm handles any weights.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: singleSourceShortestPath

nodes.label: single program multiple data
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines single program multiple data as: The dominant style of parallel programming, where all processors use the same program, though each has its own data. Also known as SPMD.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: singleprogrm

nodes.label: singularity analysis
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines singularity analysis as: A complex asymptotic technique for determining the asymptotics of certain algebraic functions.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: singularity

nodes.label: sink
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines sink as: A vertex of a directed graph with no outgoing edges . More formally, a vertex with with out-degree 0.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: sink

nodes.label: skd-tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines skd-tree as: The spatial k-d tree is a spatial access method where successive levels are split along different dimensions. Objects are indexed by their centroid , and the minimum bounding box of objects in a node are stored in the node.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: skdtree

nodes.label: skew symmetry
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines skew symmetry as: The property that the flow is the same amount, but reversed direction, starting from either vertex of every edge of a flow network . More formally, for an edge e=(v,w), f(v,w) = -f(w,v), where f(a,b) is the flow from a to b.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: skewsymmetry

nodes.label: skip list
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines skip list as: A randomized variant of an ordered linked list with additional, parallel lists. Parallel lists at higher levels skip geometrically more items. Searching begins at the highest level, to quickly get to the right part of the list, then uses progressively lower level lists. A new item is added by randomly selecting a level, then inserting it in order in the lists for that and all lower levels. With enough levels, searching is O(log n) .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: skiplist

nodes.label: Smith algorithm
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Smith algorithm as: A string matching algorithm which computes the shift value for both the rightmost character of the window and the character preceding it, then uses the maximum of the two values.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: smithAlgorithm

nodes.label: Smith-Waterman algorithm
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Smith-Waterman algorithm as: A means of searching protein databases to find those with the best alignment.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: smithWaterman

nodes.label: smoothsort
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines smoothsort as: A variant of heapsort that takes advantage of a partially ordered table. Performance is O(n) when input is sorted and O(n log n) performance for worst case .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: smoothsort

nodes.label: solvable
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines solvable as: A computational problem that can be solved by a Turing machine . The problem may have a nonbinary output.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: solvable

nodes.label: sorted array
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines sorted array as: An array whose items are kept sorted, often so searching is faster.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: sortedarray

nodes.label: sorted list
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines sorted list as: A list whose items are kept sorted.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: sortedlist

nodes.label: soundex
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines soundex as: An algorithm to code surnames phonetically by reducing them to the first letter and up to three digits, where each digit is one of six consonant sounds. This reduces matching problems from different spellings.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: soundex

nodes.label: source
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines source as: (1) A vertex of a directed graph with no incoming edges . More formally, a vertex with in-degree 0. (2) The vertex from which an edge of a directed graph leaves.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: source

nodes.label: space-constructible function
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines space-constructible function as: A function s(n) that gives the actual space used by some Turing machine on all inputs of length n.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: space

nodes.label: space ordering method
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines space ordering method as: A mapping from a discrete k-dimensional space into a linear order.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: spaceOrderingMethod

nodes.label: spanning tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines spanning tree as: A connected , acyclic subgraph containing all the vertices of a graph .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: spanningtree

nodes.label: sparse graph
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines sparse graph as: A graph in which the number of edges is much less than the possible number of edges.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: sparsegraph

nodes.label: sparse matrix
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines sparse matrix as: A matrix that has relatively few non-zero (or "interesting") entries. It may be represented in much less than n × m space.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: sparsematrix

nodes.label: sparsification
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines sparsification as: Technique for designing dynamic graph algorithms , which when applicable transform a time bound of T(n,m) onto O(T(n,n)), where m is the number of edges and n is the number of vertices of the given graph.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: sparsificatn

nodes.label: sparsity
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines sparsity as: Instances of the longest common subsequence problem in which the number of matches is small compared to the product of the lengths of the input strings.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: sparsity

nodes.label: spatial access method
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines spatial access method as: A data structure to search for lines, polygons, etc. Also known as SAM.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: spatialAccessMethod

nodes.label: square matrix
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines square matrix as: A n × n matrix , i.e., one whose size is the same in both dimensions.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: squarematrix

nodes.label: stable
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines stable as: An algorithm where the relative order upon input of items with equal keys is always preserved in the output. Usually a sort algorithm.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: stable

nodes.label: stack tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines stack tree as: A binary tree where no node , except the root , has more than one non- leaf child .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: stacktree

nodes.label: star encoding
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines star encoding as: Using a fixed dictionary , encode words in text with strings having many repeated characters, typically an asterisk or "star" (*).

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: starEncoding

nodes.label: star-shaped polygon
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines star-shaped polygon as: A polygon P in which there exists an interior point p such that all the boundary points of P are visible from p.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: starshaped

nodes.label: start state
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines start state as: An initial state or condition of a finite state machine or Turing machine . Informally, how the memory is initially set.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: startstate

nodes.label: state
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines state as: The condition of a finite state machine or Turing machine at a certain time. Informally, the content of memory.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: state

nodes.label: state machine
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines state machine as: A model of computation consisting of a (possibly infinite) set of states , a set of start states , an input alphabet , and a transition function which maps input symbols and current states to a next state . Usually understood to be a finite state machine .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: statemachine

nodes.label: static
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines static as: When the problem domain does not change.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: static

nodes.label: s-t cut
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines s-t cut as: A partitioning of the vertices of a flow network into S and T such that the source is in S and the sink is in T.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: stcut

nodes.label: st-digraph
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines st-digraph as: A directed acyclic graph with two specially marked nodes, the source s and the sink t.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: stdigraph

nodes.label: Steiner point
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Steiner point as: (1) A point that is not part of the input set of points, for instance, a point computed to construct a Steiner tree . (2) A point with a particular geometric relation to a triangle.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: steinerpoint

nodes.label: Steiner ratio
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Steiner ratio as: For a given variant of the Steiner tree problem, the maximum possible ratio of the length of a minimum spanning tree of a set of terminals to the length of an optimal Steiner tree of the same set of terminals. Usually written ρ (rho).

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: steinerratio

nodes.label: Steiner tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Steiner tree as: A minimum-weight tree connecting a designated set of vertices , called terminals , in an undirected , weighted graph or points in a space. The tree may include non-terminals, which are called Steiner vertices or Steiner points .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: steinertree

nodes.label: Steiner vertex
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Steiner vertex as: A point that is not part of the input set of points, for instance, a point computed to construct a Steiner tree .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: steinervertx

nodes.label: stooge sort
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines stooge sort as: A terribly inefficient sort algorithm that swaps the top and bottom items if needed, then ( recursively ) sorts the bottom two-thirds, then the top two-thirds, then the bottom two-thirds again.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: stoogesort

nodes.label: straight-line drawing
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines straight-line drawing as: A graph drawing in which each edge is represented by a straight line segment.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: straightline

nodes.label: strand sort
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines strand sort as: A sort algorithm that works well if many items are in order. First, begin a sublist by moving the first item from the original list to the sublist. Merge the sublist into a final, sorted list. Repeatedly extract and merge sublists until all items are sorted. Handle two or fewer items as special cases.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: strandSort

nodes.label: strictly decreasing
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines strictly decreasing as: A function from a partially ordered domain to a partially ordered range such that x < y implies f(x) > f(y).

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: strictlyDecreasing

nodes.label: strictly increasing
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines strictly increasing as: A function from a partially ordered domain to a partially ordered range such that x < y implies f(x) < f(y).

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: strictlyIncreasing

nodes.label: strictly lower triangular matrix
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines strictly lower triangular matrix as: A matrix that is only defined at (i,j) when i > j.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: strictlyLowerTriangMat

nodes.label: strictly upper triangular matrix
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines strictly upper triangular matrix as: A matrix that is only defined at (i,j) when i < j.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: strictlyUpperTriangMat

nodes.label: string
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines string as: A list of characters, usually implemented as an array . Informally a word, phrase, sentence, etc. Since text processing is so common, a special type with substring operations is often available.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: string

nodes.label: string matching with errors
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines string matching with errors as: Searching for approximate (e.g., up to a predefined number of symbol mismatches, insertions, and deletions) occurrences of a pattern string in a text string. Preprocessing, e.g., building an index, may or may not be allowed. Also known as approximate string matching.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: stringMatchwError

nodes.label: string matching with mismatches
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines string matching with mismatches as: The special case of string matching with errors where mismatches are the only type of error allowed.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: stringMatchwMismatch

nodes.label: string editing problem
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines string editing problem as: The problem of finding an edit script of minimum cost which transforms a given string into another given string.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: stringedit

nodes.label: strip packing
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines strip packing as: Pack a set of rectangles into a strip of width 1 to minimize the height used. Rectangles may not overlap or be rotated. Without loss of generality, the height of rectangles is at most 1. This is NP-hard .

nodes.label: zipper
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines zipper as: A data structure equivalent to a binary tree that is "opened" so that some node is accessible. It consists of a pair: the current node, along with information to reconstruct the tree. Reconstruction information is called the path or context. A move-to-left-child operation returns the left subtree, along with a new path, which has (i) a Left value, (ii) the current node, (iii) the right subtree, and (iv) any previous path. A similar operation moves to the right child. A move-up operation returns a tree rebuilt from the path information and the current node, along with the previous path.

nodes.label: ZPP
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines ZPP as: The class of languages for which a membership computation by a probabilistic Turing machine halts in polynomial time with no false acceptances or rejections, but randomly some "I don't know" answers. "ZPP" means " Z ero error P robability in P olynomial" time. Formal Definition: For a language, S, there exists a probabilistic Turing machine , M, that halts in polynomial time . M (correctly) accepts or rejects the string or, randomly, halts in an "I don't know" state.

nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes huge sparse array as: Store unique-key items using an item array large enough for the items and an uninitialized location array covering the much larger key range. Insertion records the next item position in the location array. Lookup validates the stored position against the number of inserted items and checks the item's key. Keys must be unique; duplicate keys require collision resolution. NIST reports linear total insertion and listing time, and constant lookup time, assuming constant-time allocation.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: hugeSparseArray

nodes.label: hypergraph
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes hypergraph as: A graph whose undirected hyperedges connect two or more vertices. It consists of a vertex set and a collection of hyperedges, each of which is a set of vertices.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: hypergraph

nodes.label: HyperLogLog
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes HyperLogLog as: Estimate the number of distinct items by hashing each item, using initial hash bits to select a counter and updating that counter using the remaining hash bits. After processing the items, the procedure uses a harmonic mean derived from leading-zero counts to form the estimate.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: hyperloglog

nodes.label: inclusion-exclusion principle
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes inclusion-exclusion principle as: A rule for computing the probability of exactly a specified number of occurrences among a collection of events.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: inclusion

nodes.label: inverse Ackermann function
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes inverse Ackermann function as: A two-parameter function whose value grows very slowly. NIST cautions that it is not strictly the inverse of Ackermann's function; its growth is described as slow in comparison with Ackermann's rapid growth.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: inverseAckermann

nodes.label: jump list
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes jump list as: A sorted doubly linked list with two additional levels of links spanning geometrically increasing distances.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: jumpList

nodes.label: knapsack problem
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes knapsack problem as: Given items with different values and volumes, find the most valuable set that fits a knapsack of fixed volume. Each item is either taken or not taken. NIST also calls this the zero-one or binary knapsack problem.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: knapsackProblem

nodes.label: kth order Fibonacci numbers
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes kth order Fibonacci numbers as: A sequence in which each number is the sum of the k preceding numbers. The usual Fibonacci numbers are the case k equals two.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: kthOrderFibonacci

nodes.label: kth shortest path
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes kth shortest path as: Find the kth shortest path from one graph vertex to another. Variants may require edge-disjoint or vertex-disjoint paths; shortest may mean fewest edges or least total weight.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: kthShortestPath

nodes.label: layered graph
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes layered graph as: A connected graph whose vertices are partitioned into layers. Edges have nonnegative integer weights and connect only vertices in successive layers. Its width is the largest number of vertices in any layer.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: layeredgraph

nodes.label: linear
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes linear as: In one sense, a constant times the argument plus a constant. In complexity theory, a measure of computation, usually execution time or memory, bounded by a linear function of problem size.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: linear

nodes.label: linear congruential generator
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes linear congruential generator as: A class of pseudorandom number generators that compute each number from the current one using a linear congruence. The current number is multiplied by a constant, another constant is added, and the result is reduced modulo a modulus; NIST requires the multiplier and modulus to be relatively prime.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: linearCongruentGen

nodes.label: linear hashing
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes linear hashing as: A dynamic hash table that grows one slot at a time. Its family of hash functions has ranges that double between successive functions. A split pointer tracks slots already split; splitting a slot and advancing the pointer maintains the load factor. After the pointer reaches the end, the ranges double and the pointer starts over.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: linearHashing

nodes.label: linear probing sort
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes linear probing sort as: Distribute items into a larger array according to interpolation of their keys, putting collisions into the next empty location, then pack the items into an array of the original size. Extra space at the end handles overflow, but NIST states that the sort may fail if that overflow space is exceeded.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: linearProbingSort

nodes.label: linear program
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes linear program as: An optimization problem that minimizes a vector-dot-product objective subject to componentwise linear inequalities and nonnegative decision variables.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: linearProgramming

nodes.label: L_m distance
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes L_m distance as: A generalized distance between two points, also called Minkowski distance. NIST identifies Euclidean distance with the member indexed by two and rectilinear or Manhattan distance with the member indexed by one.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: lmdistance

nodes.label: Lotka's law
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes Lotka's law as: A power law relating the number of authors to their number of contributions, often nearly an inverse-square law.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: lotkaslaw

nodes.label: matrix multiplication
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes matrix multiplication as: A binary operation on two matrices, requiring the first matrix's column count to equal the second matrix's row count. The product has the first matrix's row count and the second matrix's column count.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: matrixMultiply

nodes.label: merge
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes merge as: Combine two or more sorted sequences of data into a single sorted sequence.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: merge

nodes.label: Miller-Rabin
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes Miller-Rabin as: A heuristic primality test that repeatedly checks pseudoprimality to randomly chosen bases and whether square roots of one modulo the tested number are trivial. Some composite numbers may be incorrectly judged prime.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: millerRabin

nodes.label: moderately exponential
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes moderately exponential as: Growth in a measure of computation, usually execution time or memory, that exceeds every polynomial but is slower than every exponential with base greater than one.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: moderatexpon

nodes.label: multiplication method
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes multiplication method as: A hash function based on multiplying a key by an irrational number between zero and one, or an approximation to it. The modulo-one operation removes the integer part of that product.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: multiplicationMethod

nodes.label: NC many-one reducibility
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes NC many-one reducibility as: One language is NC many-one reducible to another when a function in FNC maps an input into the second language if and only if that input belongs to the first.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: nCmanyone

nodes.label: optimal merge
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes optimal merge as: Merge sorted sequences of different lengths into one output while minimizing reads, merging only two sequences at a time. At each step merge the two shortest sequences and repeat until one remains.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: optimalMerge

nodes.label: parallel prefix computation
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes parallel prefix computation as: Compute an associative function over every prefix of an array in parallel. For an n-element array, NIST reports Θ(n) processors and Θ(log n) time. Parallel iterations must read the old array values before overwriting them; input values can first be copied to a result array in parallel.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: parallelPrefix

nodes.label: partition
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes partition as: In one sense, divide a set into nonempty disjoint subsets that together cover the original set. In another, rearrange array elements into two or more groups, typically separating values below and above a chosen value.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: partition

nodes.label: Patricia tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes Patricia tree as: A compact trie representation that merges a node that is an only child with its parent. NIST's note uses radix tree for a binary Patricia tree.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: patriciatree

nodes.label: P-complete
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes P-complete as: Under NC reducibility, a language is P-complete if it belongs to P and is P-hard.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: pcomplete

nodes.label: perfect k-ary tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes perfect k-ary tree as: A k-ary tree with all leaf nodes at the same depth and all internal nodes of degree k. NIST notes that authors differ in their terminology.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: perfectKaryTree

nodes.label: polyhedron
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes polyhedron as: The solution set of a finite system of linear inequalities on real-valued variables.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: polyhedron

nodes.label: polylogarithmic
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes polylogarithmic as: In one sense, a sum of constant multiples of powers of a logarithm of the argument. In complexity theory, a measure of computation bounded by a polylogarithmic function of problem size.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: polylogarith

nodes.label: polynomial
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes polynomial as: In one sense, a sum of constant multiples of powers of the argument. In complexity theory, a measure of computation bounded by a polynomial function of problem size.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: polynomial

nodes.label: quadtree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes quadtree as: A tree in which each node is split along every dimension. NIST notes that the original two-dimensional picture representation gave each node four children.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: quadtree

nodes.label: quadtree complexity theorem
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes quadtree complexity theorem as: For quadtree representations of simple polygons with nonintersecting edges and no holes, NIST reports that node count is proportional to perimeter when the image-resolution term in its bound is negligible. It also reports an analogous three-dimensional statement with surface area replacing perimeter.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: quadtreecplx

nodes.label: select kth element
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes select kth element as: Find the kth smallest element of a set. NIST describes modified distribution sort and select-and-partition as two approaches and also calls this the selection problem.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: selectkth

nodes.label: set cover
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes set cover as: A collection of sets whose union covers the members of the full collection's union. The set-cover problem seeks a collection of minimum size.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: setcover

nodes.label: spiral storage
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes spiral storage as: A dynamic hash table that grows a few slots at a time and uses a hash function with range from zero inclusive to one exclusive.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: spiralStorage

nodes.label: tabulation hashing
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes tabulation hashing as: Compute a hash value by XORing values drawn from tables indexed by the input characters.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: tabulationHashing

nodes.label: taco sort
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes taco sort as: A deliberately inefficient sorting algorithm that repeatedly changes a random item by a random amount until a sorted permutation occurs.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: tacoSort

nodes.label: Θ
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes Θ as: An asymptotically tight execution-resource bound: for all sufficiently large problem sizes, a function lies between two fixed positive constant multiples of the comparison function. The constants and size threshold must not depend on problem size.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: theta

nodes.label: towers of Hanoi
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes towers of Hanoi as: Given three posts and disks of decreasing sizes, move the disks from one post to another one at a time without placing a larger disk on a smaller disk.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: towersOfHanoi

nodes.label: twisted tabulation hashing
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes twisted tabulation hashing as: A tabulation-hashing variant in which a table is indexed by the XOR of the last character and a twister value obtained from the rest of the string. NIST notes that the first character may instead be treated specially.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: twistedTabulationHashing

nodes.label: 2-choice hashing
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes 2-choice hashing as: A hash-table variant that hashes each key with two hash functions and places it at the position containing fewer colliding keys. A collision-resolution scheme is needed unless keys are kept in buckets.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: twoChoiceHashing

nodes.label: 2-left hashing
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes 2-left hashing as: A dictionary implemented with two equal-sized hash tables and two different hash functions. Put a new key in the second table only when its candidate position has fewer colliding keys than the first table's position; ties go to the first table.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: twoLeftHashing

nodes.label: unbounded knapsack problem
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes unbounded knapsack problem as: Given item types with different values and volumes, find the most valuable set that fits a fixed-volume knapsack, with no bound on the count of each type. NIST describes this as an NP-hard combinatorial optimization problem.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: unboundedKnapsack

nodes.label: Zipf's law
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes Zipf's law as: A distribution of word or item occurrence probabilities in which a few items occur very often and many occur rarely.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: zipfslaw

nodes.label: Benford's law
nodes.summary: NIST DADS reports Benford's law as follows: On a wide variety of statistical data, the probability that the first digit is d is the base-ten logarithm of one plus the reciprocal of d.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: benfordslaw

nodes.label: Kraft's inequality
nodes.summary: NIST DADS states Kraft's inequality for a binary tree: Sum, over all its leaves, two raised to the negative depth of each leaf. That sum is at most one.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: kraftsinqlty

nodes.label: linear product
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes a linear product of two vectors using suitable operations ⊗ and ⊕. For each output index k from zero through m+n, combine under ⊕ the terms X[i] ⊗ Y[j] whose indices satisfy i+j=k. The printed result has components Z[0] through Z[m+n].

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: linearprodct

nodes.label: slope selection
nodes.summary: Katz and Sharir's original publication abstract defines slope selection as: Given n points in the plane and an integer k, find the pair of points whose connecting line has the kth smallest slope.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: slopeselectn
Katz and Sharir: Optimal Slope Selection via Expanders — institutional publication abstract

nodes.label: Stirling's approximation
nodes.summary: NIST DADS gives Stirling's approximation for large values of n: n! ≈ (n/e)^n * sqrt(2*n*pi). Here ^ denotes exponentiation.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: stirlingsApproximation

nodes.label: Stirling's formula
nodes.summary: NIST DADS gives the following Stirling bounds for large values of n. Set S = (n/e)^n * sqrt(2*n*pi); then S < n! < S * (1 + 1/(12*n-1)). Here ^ denotes exponentiation.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: stirlingsFormula

nodes.label: bucket array
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes bucket array as: A dictionary implementation using an array indexed by the keys of the dictionary items.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bucketarray

nodes.label: cube root
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes cube root as: A manual, long-hand method of extracting cube roots, described by NIST DADS as similar to long-hand division or its manual square-root method. This scoped description does not reproduce the numerical worked example.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: cubeRoot

nodes.label: square root
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes square root as: A manual, long-hand method of extracting square roots, described by NIST DADS as similar to long-hand division. This scoped description does not reproduce the numerical worked example.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: squareRoot

nodes.label: Big Omega (asymptotic lower bound)
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes Big Omega (asymptotic lower bound) as: An asymptotic lower bound in which, beyond some fixed input size, a function is at least a positive constant multiple of the comparison function. Both constants are fixed independently of input size. NIST distinguishes this all-sufficiently-large-inputs definition from a weaker traditional definition requiring only an unbounded sequence of such inputs.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: omegaCapital

nodes.label: R+-tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes R+-tree as: A height-balanced spatial access method that splits space into hierarchically nested boxes and indexes an object in each box intersecting it.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rplustree

nodes.label: R*-tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes R*-tree as: A height-balanced spatial access method with hierarchically nested, possibly overlapping boxes. NIST describes it as similar to an R-tree but reinserting entries on overflow rather than splitting.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rstartree

nodes.label: shortest path
nodes.summary: NIST DADS describes shortest path as: The single-pair shortest-path problem seeks the shortest-path weight or distance between graph vertices, using measures such as edge count or total edge weight. NIST distinguishes this value problem from reconstructing the route itself, which requires an algorithm modification.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: shortestpath

support.quote:
Title:
A Spin Entanglement Witness for Quantum Gravity
[Submitted on 19 Jul 2017]

Here, we introduce an idea for such a test based on the principle that two objects cannot be entangled without a quantum mediator. We show that despite the weakness of gravity, the phase evolution induced by the gravitational interaction of two micron size test masses in adjacent matter-wave interferometers can detectably entangle them even when they are placed far apart enough to keep Casimir-Polder forces at bay. We provide a prescription for witnessing this entanglement, which certifies gravity as a quantum coherent mediator, through simple correlation measurements between two spins: one embedded in each test mass.

Subjects:
Quantum Physics (quant-ph)
; General Relativity and Quantum Cosmology (gr-qc); High Energy Physics - Theory (hep-th)

support.quote:
Title:
Dark Matter Search Results from 4.2 Tonne-Years of Exposure of the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) Experiment

We report results of a search for nuclear recoils induced by weakly interacting massive particle (WIMP) dark matter using the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) two-phase xenon time projection chamber. This analysis uses a total exposure of $4.2\pm0.1$ tonne-years from 280 live days of LZ operation, of which $3.3\pm0.1$ tonne-years and 220 live days are new.
After removal of artificial signal-like events injected into the data set to mitigate analyzer bias, we find no evidence for an excess over expected backgrounds.

Subjects:
High Energy Physics - Experiment (hep-ex)

decisions.rationale: The retained primary source describes the studied spheroidal-to-lenticular microstructure suite and interprets it as silicified and pyritized vesicular volcanic glass using size distribution, wall ultrastructure and chemistry. The candidate accurately attributes this interpretation to the study. Kind, domain and neutral representation metadata are justified without identifying unrelated fossils as the same objects.
decisions.limitations: The abiogenic interpretation concerns the examined Dresser sample suite. It neither disproves every reported Archean microfossil nor automatically invalidates separate Dresser biosignatures.

decisions.rationale: The 2018 Dresser source explicitly reports kerogenous material associated with much altered volcanic glass, carbon lining/filling some vesicles, and organic-rich laminae enclosing multiple vesicles. These are associations, represented as such. The claim label, earth-domain scope, sampled-material identity and standalone placement match the retained article and neutral policy.
decisions.limitations: Associated kerogenous carbon does not by itself establish whether vesicles, laminae or carbon are biological.

decisions.rationale: The exact excerpt reports kerogenous material associated with altered volcanic glass, organic carbon lining or filling some vesicles, and organic-rich laminae surrounding multiple vesicles. The candidate preserves the observed association and its limited population. Claim/earth and neutral metadata are justified; no additional identity or classification is proposed.
decisions.limitations: Organic carbon accompanying volcanic structures does not demonstrate that the structures themselves are biological or establish the origin of the associated carbon.

decisions.rationale: The article warns that reworked, isolated silicified microstructures of the studied volcanic-glass type can adsorb carbon and become pyritized, confusing life-detection interpretation; in those cases nanoscale wall analysis is required to exclude a biological origin. The candidate weakens 'required' to 'may be required' but does not strengthen it; its scope is explicitly conditional. Earth-domain claim and neutral metadata fit.
decisions.limitations: Methodological warning is conditional for these volcanic-glass-like isolated structures, not a universal nanoscale requirement for every candidate biosignature.

decisions.rationale: The source explicitly warns that reworked isolated silicified structures of the studied type can adsorb carbon and become pyritized, creating difficulties in microfossil identification. The candidate retains the single-species laboratory context and limiting condition. Claim/earth, reported, undated and frontier=false are appropriate, with no asserted relationship or identity merge.
decisions.limitations: The experiments used Burkholderia fungorum under controlled laboratory conditions with added glucose and low-salt medium. The result does not establish the same response across natural microbial communities, seawater or all basalt environments.

decisions.rationale: The retained 2018 source directly says dissolved major-element concentrations in biotic synthetic-basalt-glass colonization experiments increased with increasing residual stress and Fe(II) content. The candidate represents an association over the tested glasses, not separately isolated causation. Claim classification, earth domain, lab scope, descriptive comparison direction and neutral metadata are faithful.
decisions.limitations: Residual stress and Fe(II) vary across the reported treatments, so individual independent causal contributions cannot be inferred.

decisions.rationale: The retained source explicitly reports that dissolved major-element concentrations in biotic synthetic-basalt-glass colonization assays increased with residual stress and Fe(II) content. The candidate treats the finding as a reported laboratory association and preserves its joint-factor limitation. Claim/earth and neutral metadata are justified without additional placement or relations.

decisions.rationale: The source directly contrasts intensely biofilm-covered synthetic basalt glasses with residual stress and high Fe(II) against sparse colonization on unstressed, high-Fe(III) glasses. The statement and label retain both coupled conditions and comparison direction. Earth-domain claim, laboratory scope, independent placement and neutral metadata are justified.

assertions.statement: Turner et al. (2015) stated that the Ara−3 Cit− lineage extinction cause remained unknown, rejected their initial ongoing Cit+ adaptation explanation, and proposed an unidentified rare perturbation as a possible cause rather than an observed event.

scope.population: Ara−3 Cit− ecological lineage extinction between generation 43,500 and 44,000
scope.time: Authors’ 2015 interpretation of extinction and replay results
scope.assumptions: Reasoning combines failed replay repeatability, reinvasion, population-size argument, and hypothetical perturbation, not direct observation of a catastrophe.

support.quote:
The cause of the Cit
−
lineage’s extinction remains unknown. We have rejected our initial hypothesis that on-going adaptation of the Cit
+
bacteria caused the extinction. A purely stochastic extinction of the Cit
−
lineage is also extremely unlikely.

We propose, therefore, that the cause of the Cit
−
extinction was a “random catastrophe”, that is, a large, rare event that reduced the size of the Ara–3 population as a whole or, at least, the Cit
−
lineage within it. We do not know the nature of this random catastrophe, but it could have been some unusual variation in laboratory conditions, such as soap residue in a flask or a problem with the deionized water used to make the culture medium.

decisions.rationale: The retained Leon passage locates rudimentary citrate utilization in Ara−3 after 31,500 LTEE generations and more complete citrate use in its descendants by 33,000. The summary attributes the chronology to the authors and distinguishes Cit+ from Cit++; claim kind, life domain, neutral metadata, and independent node identity fit. No relationship or taxonomy placement is proposed.
decisions.limitations: This is a historical report, not direct observation of the first Cit+ cell, and it cannot establish similar changes in the other eleven populations.

decisions.rationale: The retained Leon et al. (2018) source explicitly identifies the Ara−3 LTEE population, reports emergence of citrate utilization after 31,500 generations, and distinguishes this initial phenotype from descendants able to fully exploit citrate by 33,000 generations. The claim's identity, label, life domain, kind and bounded chronology are justified. Status reported attributes the historical account to its source; undated and frontier=false make no positive chronology-classification or currency assertion. No identity merge, taxonomy placement or graph relation is proposed.
decisions.limitations: The first successful Cit+ cell was not directly observed. The historical chronology does not establish identical evolution in the other eleven LTEE populations. The other retained source captures do not supply additional independent evidence for this assertion.

decisions.rationale: Leon reports a 2.2% competitive fitness advantage for ZDB564 versus its Cit− revertant ZDB706 attributable to the citT-activating duplication. The complete label, strains, effect, life-domain claim representation, and reported/undated/frontier=false metadata match the source.
decisions.limitations: The estimate is specific to this evolved background and assay, not proof that citT activation generally increases fitness.

decisions.rationale: Leon et al. directly report a 2.2% competitive fitness advantage associated with the citT-activating duplication in ZDB564 relative to its Cit− revertant ZDB706. Both strain identities and the measured effect are preserved. The life-domain claim node represents one specific experimental result, with neutral scientific metadata and no unsupported relationship or placement.
decisions.limitations: The comparison applies to this evolved genetic background and DM-medium competition assay. Arabinose-marker controls address a potential experimental confound but do not establish that activating citT universally increases fitness. The advantage should not be conflated with the later Cit++ refinement phenotype.

decisions.rationale: The REL606 engineered P_rnk-citT versus null-cassette assay directly reports a 1.0% advantage with one-tailed P=0.033 and n=12, described as weak evidence near assay precision. The candidate explicitly calls the activation engineered, and its kind, domain, neutral metadata and independent identity are justified.
decisions.limitations: The knock-in mimics but is not the original tandem duplication; neither a robust benefit nor actual Cit+ evolution in the ancestor is established.

decisions.rationale: The source reports an engineered P_rnk-citT knock-in comparison in ancestral strain REL606, a measured 1.0% fitness advantage, one-tailed P=0.033 and n=12. It explicitly characterizes the statistical evidence as relatively weak because the effect approaches assay resolution. The canonical summary preserves both the engineering intervention and uncertainty; claim kind, life domain, independent identity and neutral metadata are justified.
decisions.limitations: A chromosomal knock-in mimicking citT activation is not the naturally evolved rnk-citG tandem duplication. The result does not show that Cit+ spontaneously evolved in ancestral REL606, that the advantage was robust, or that it was sufficient to survive competition against alternative beneficial mutations.

decisions.rationale: Leon reports disadvantageous citT activation in 11 of 23 additional evolved pre-Cit+ clones, including five losses exceeding 20%. The sampled population, numerical counts, claim label, life domain, neutral representation, and lack of proposed graph edges are appropriate.
decisions.limitations: The result uses selected clones and statistical tests; it cannot be generalized to all genetic backgrounds or other LTEE populations.

decisions.rationale: Leon et al. describe testing 23 additional evolved pre-Cit+ clones and report a competitive disadvantage following citT activation in 11, including five disadvantages greater than 20%, evaluated using one-tailed bootstrap tests. The candidate retains the sampled-clone denominator, direction of the effect and distinction between rudimentary Cit+ and refined Cit++. Claim kind, life domain, identity, standalone placement and neutral metadata are appropriate.
decisions.limitations: The 23 clones are a selected sample from one LTEE population, not all historical genetic backgrounds. Fitness effects may depend on private mutations and environmental conditions. The experiments do not prove that every possible route to citrate utilization was inaccessible in those backgrounds.

decisions.rationale: The authors explicitly report the pooled −5.4% estimate and [−7.2%, −3.6%] interval for ZDB425, ZDB458 and ZDB464. The record confines interpretation to the tested intermediate phylogenetic group, with the named isolates and lineage caveats.
decisions.limitations: The authors allow for unobserved changes between sampled generations; the responsible mutations are not experimentally identified by this estimate.

decisions.rationale: The retained phylogenetic analysis explicitly groups ZDB425, ZDB458 and ZDB464 and reports an estimated fitness effect of −5.4% with interval [−7.2%, −3.6%]. The canonical representation identifies a grouped intermediate-lineage estimate rather than treating the number as an individual-clone effect. The life-domain claim classification, attribution, neutral status and separate node identity are justified; no relationship direction or taxonomy is asserted.
decisions.limitations: The group estimate does not identify the causative genetic changes. ZDB425 and ZDB458 have private mutations, and the authors cannot exclude further changes along the main lineage between sampling points. The interval must not be generalized into a continuously measured effect across 10,000 generations.

decisions.rationale: Leon identifies ZDB19 and ZDB13 among the later fully potentiated pre-Cit+ lineage as early as 29,000 generations, reporting an overall +2.4% fitness estimate with 95% confidence interval [+1.4%, +3.4%]. The scope, label, classification as a life-domain claim, and neutral metadata preserve source meaning.
decisions.limitations: The pooled engineered-activation result does not demonstrate Cit+ cells already existed at generation 29,000, identify causative mutations, or guarantee evolutionary success.

decisions.rationale: Leon et al. identify ZDB19 and ZDB13 as members of a later fully potentiated pre-Cit+ group represented as early as 29,000 generations. They report a group fitness effect of +2.4%, with 95% confidence interval [+1.4%, +3.4%]. The candidate preserves the group-level estimate, time qualifier, biological lineage and distinction between engineered activation and historical Cit+ appearance. Kind, domain, identity, neutral metadata and standalone representation are supported.
decisions.limitations: The grouped estimate does not prove that Cit+ organisms were already present at generation 29,000, identify a specific potentiating mutation, or show that an initially beneficial mutant would inevitably establish in the evolving population.

decisions.rationale: The revised label correctly identifies the evolved generation-31,000 Ara−3 population, rather than the founding ancestor. Leon explicitly describes equally mixed engineered Cit+ and Cit− ZDB706 variants at about 1% combined frequency, a 0.9% Cit+ advantage and no support for the tested ecological-potentiation hypothesis. The attribution, scope, kind, life domain, neutral metadata and independent identity are justified.
decisions.limitations: P=0.053 for difference from pairwise competitions is marginal. The narrow experiment does not rule out all frequency-dependent or other ecological effects.

decisions.rationale: The revised canonical label correctly specifies an evolved generation-31,000 Ara−3 population mixture, not the ancestral founding population. Leon et al. report introducing equally mixed Cit+ and Cit− engineered ZDB706 variants at approximately 1% combined frequency into that evolved population and measuring a 0.9% Cit+ fitness advantage. The authors explicitly report no support for the ecological-potentiation hypothesis tested. Source identity, experimental population, comparison direction, life domain, claim kind and neutral metadata are preserved.
decisions.limitations: The difference from ordinary pairwise competition was marginal, with two-tailed P=0.053. A negative result in this particular mixture does not exclude other forms of ecological potentiation, frequency dependence or population interactions. The engineered variants were not the original founding strains. The revised candidate must be reviewed on its own merits rather than accepted because an earlier version was rejected.

decisions.rationale: Turner's retained source reports Cit−-specific PCR bands and phenotypic detection through 43,500 generations, without detection at 44,000 or later sampled time points. The node expressly says 'detectable', so it does not turn a screening result into proof of absolute extinction; its claim kind, life domain, source attribution and neutral metadata are justified.
decisions.limitations: PCR and phenotypic screening have detection limits, and the source does not reveal the precise instant or mechanism of lineage loss.

decisions.rationale: The retained Turner et al. (2015) source reports Cit−-specific PCR detection through 43,500 generations, no amplification from 44,000 generations onward, and matching phenotypic screening results in the sampled cultures. The candidate describes loss of detectable genotype and phenotype, not observation of every individual organism's disappearance. Its life-domain claim identity, bounded historical scope and neutral scientific metadata are justified.
decisions.limitations: Negative PCR and phenotypic screens are constrained by sampling and detection sensitivity. They do not establish an exact extinction time within the 500-generation interval or exclude an undetected residual Cit− population. No causal mechanism follows from disappearance alone.

decisions.rationale: The retained Turner passage states that Cit− persisted in all 20 replays started at generation 43,500 and all 20 at generation 40,000 after 500 generations, plus one 43,000-generation culture followed for 2,500 generations. Counts, timeframes, node identity and neutral reported status agree with the source.
decisions.limitations: The single extended culture is additional to the 40 short replays. Persistence in these replays does not establish survival under every possible prior environmental disturbance.

decisions.rationale: Turner et al. report Cit− persistence in all 20 independently propagated replays founded from generation 43,500 and all 20 controls founded from generation 40,000 after 500 generations. They separately report persistence in one generation-43,000 culture extended for 2,500 generations. The candidate preserves the three starting conditions, replicate counts, propagation durations and observed outcome. Claim kind, life domain, standalone identity and neutral metadata are justified.
decisions.limitations: The one extended replay is separate from the 40 shorter replays. Failure to reproduce extinction under standard conditions does not prove competitive extinction impossible or reproduce an unidentified historical laboratory perturbation. The candidate does not establish a universal survival guarantee.

decisions.rationale: Turner explicitly reports that a 43,000-generation Cit− clone invaded the 50,000-generation Ara−3 resident population and reached roughly 3 × 10^5 cells/mL, about tenfold below other treatments. The candidate preserves generation direction, measurement unit and the mean across high- and low-density starts. Kind, domain and neutral metadata are suitable.
decisions.limitations: The assay spans seven days, and invasion under these conditions does not show indefinite stable coexistence or resolve the earlier extinction.

decisions.rationale: The Turner source explicitly states that a generation-43,000 Cit− clone invaded a resident generation-50,000 population and reports a final mean Cit− density of approximately 3 × 10^5 cells/mL, about an order of magnitude below densities in the other treatments. The candidate preserves which population supplied the invading clone, which was the recipient, and the quantitative result. Life-domain claim identity, neutral metadata and independent representation are justified.
decisions.limitations: The measured density is the mean across high- and low-inoculum treatments in a short competition experiment. Successful reinvasion does not establish indefinite stable coexistence, an invariant ecological equilibrium or the cause of the original Cit− loss. The source does not justify reversing the invasion direction.

decisions.rationale: Turner explicitly states that the Cit− extinction cause remains unknown, rejects the authors' initial ongoing Cit+ adaptation explanation, and offers an unidentified rare random catastrophe as a proposed explanation. The node attributes the hypothesis, does not assert an observed catastrophe, and preserves the scoped historical uncertainty, life domain, kind and neutral metadata.
decisions.limitations: Proposed events such as residue or water issues were not observed. The evidence does not eliminate every possible ecological or fitness-related extinction mechanism.

decisions.rationale: Turner et al. explicitly state that the cause of Ara−3 Cit− lineage extinction remains unknown. They reject their initial ongoing-Cit+ adaptation explanation and propose a rare random catastrophe as a possible account, while acknowledging that its nature is unknown. The candidate clearly marks the perturbation as proposed rather than observed. The claim kind, life domain, historical attribution, neutral status, unresolved era, frontier=false and independent identity are justified.
decisions.limitations: The source does not demonstrate that a random catastrophe occurred, establish a particular laboratory error, or eliminate every conceivable fitness-mediated or ecological explanation. The rejection applies to the authors' original tested explanation, not all possible evolutionary models. No identity, taxonomy or graph relationship is independently established by this record.

support.quote: We analyze the performance of language models on two tasks that require identifying relevant information in their input contexts: multi-document question answering and key-value retrieval.

In particular, we observe that performance is often highest when relevant information occurs at the beginning or end of the input context, and significantly degrades when models must access relevant information in the middle of long contexts, even for explicitly long-context models.

support.quote: We evaluate 17 long-context LMs with 13 representative tasks in RULER. support.quote: To this end, we propose CoF (Coarse to Fine), a novel pipeline that utilizes off-the-shelf LLMs to automatically generate long-context QA instances with precise sentence-level citations, and leverage this pipeline to construct LongCite-45k, a large-scale SFT dataset for LQAC. decisions.rationale: The retained Lost in the Middle abstract explicitly identifies multi-document question answering and key-value retrieval as the two evaluated tasks. decisions.limitations: The retained abstract provides no numerical positional effect size, confidence interval, complete model roster, or evidence about models released after the evaluation. The reported effect is task-dependent rather than universal.

decisions.rationale: Both tasks and the beginning/end-versus-middle positional pattern are explicitly reported in Liu et al.'s retained abstract. 'Often' and 'can degrade' preserve nonuniversal task-specific behavior. This is a source-attributed information-domain claim, not a current-model capability claim; neutral reported/undated/frontier=false metadata are correctly used. decisions.limitations: This is a historical evaluation on two retrieval-oriented tasks; the captured abstract supplies no model-by-position numerical table, effect size, or proof about every long-context model. It cannot establish current-model behavior or all kinds of long-context reasoning.

decisions.rationale: The retained RULER abstract describes a configurable synthetic benchmark, variations in needle type and quantity, multi-hop tracing, aggregation, and an evaluation involving 17 language models and 13 representative tasks. decisions.rationale: RULER's retained abstract explicitly describes needle variation, multi-hop tracing, aggregation, and evaluation of 17 models on 13 tasks. Configurability and synthetic-task limits are preserved. decisions.limitations: All 13 tasks are synthetic; the abstract does not establish that they exhaust downstream workloads or reliably predict real-document performance. The 17 tested models cannot be generalized to all models.

decisions.rationale: The retained RULER abstract states that the evaluated 17 models claimed context capacities of at least 32K tokens, that almost all experienced large performance declines as input length increased, and that only half maintained satisfactory performance at 32K despite nearly perfect vanilla needle-retrieval accuracy. decisions.limitations: Satisfactory performance is the authors' benchmark-specific criterion.
