support.quote: Searching for axion dark matter, the ADMX collaboration acquired data from January to October 2018, over the mass range 2.81--3.31 $\mu$eV, corresponding to the frequency range 680--790 MHz. Using an axion haloscope consisting of a microwave cavity in a strong magnetic field, the ADMX experiment excluded Dine-Fischler-Srednicki-Zhitnisky (DFSZ) axions at 100% dark matter density over this entire frequency range, except for a few gaps due to mode crossings. This paper explains the full ADMX analysis for Run 1B, motivating analysis choices informed by details specific to this run.

We constrain the abundance of primordial black holes (PBH) using 2622 microlensing events obtained from 5-years observations of stars in the Galactic bulge by the Optical Gravitational Lensing Experiment (OGLE). The majority of microlensing events display a single or at least continuous population that has a peak around the light curve timescale $t_{\rm E}\simeq 20~{\rm days}$ and a wide distribution over the range $t_{\rm E}\simeq [1, 300]~{\rm days}$, while the data also indicates a second population of 6 ultrashort-timescale events in $t_{\rm E}\simeq [0.1,0.3]~{\rm days}$, which are advocated to be due to free-floating planets. We confirm that the main population of OGLE events can be well modeled by microlensing due to brown dwarfs, main sequence stars and stellar remnants (white dwarfs and neutron stars) in the standard Galactic bulge and disk models for their spatial and velocity distributions. Using the dark matter (DM) model for the Milky Way (MW) halo relative to the Galactic bulge/disk models, we obtain the tightest upper bound on the PBH abundance in the mass range $M_{\rm PBH}\simeq[10^{-6},10^{-3}]M_\odot$ (Earth-Jupiter mass range), if we employ null hypothesis that the OGLE data does not contain any PBH microlensing event. More interestingly, we also show that Earth-mass PBHs can well reproduce the 6 ultrashort-timescale events, without the need of free-floating planets, if the mass fraction of PBH to DM is at a per cent level, which is consistent with other constraints such as the microlensing search for Andromeda galaxy (M31) and the longer timescale OGLE events. Our result gives a hint of PBH existence, and can be confirmed or falsified by microlensing search for stars in M31, because M31 is towards the MW halo direction and should therefore contain a much less number of free-floating planets, even if exist, than the direction to the MW center.

We report results of a search for nuclear recoils induced by weakly interacting massive particle (WIMP) dark matter using the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) two-phase xenon time projection chamber. This analysis uses a total exposure of $4.2\pm0.1$ tonne-years from 280 live days of LZ operation, of which $3.3\pm0.1$ tonne-years and 220 live days are new. A technique to actively tag background electronic recoils from $^{214}$Pb $\beta$ decays is featured for the first time. Enhanced electron-ion recombination is observed in two-neutrino double electron capture decays of $^{124}$Xe, representing a noteworthy new background. After removal of artificial signal-like events injected into the data set to mitigate analyzer bias, we find no evidence for an excess over expected backgrounds. World-leading constraints are placed on spin-independent (SI) and spin-dependent WIMP-nucleon cross sections for masses $\geq$9 GeV/$c^2$. The strongest SI exclusion set is $2.2\times10^{-48}$ cm$^{2}$ at the 90% confidence level and the best SI median sensitivity achieved is $5.1\times10^{-48}$ cm$^{2}$, both for a mass of 40 GeV/$c^2$.

We present constraints on the masses of extremely light bosons dubbed fuzzy dark matter from Lyman-$\alpha$ forest data. Extremely light bosons with a De Broglie wavelength of $\sim 1$ kpc have been suggested as dark matter candidates that may resolve some of the current small scale problems of the cold dark matter model. For the first time we use hydrodynamical simulations to model the Lyman-$\alpha$ flux power spectrum in these models and compare with the observed flux power spectrum from two different data sets: the XQ-100 and HIRES/MIKE quasar spectra samples. After marginalization over nuisance and physical parameters and with conservative assumptions for the thermal history of the IGM that allow for jumps in the temperature of up to $5000\rm\,K$, XQ-100 provides a lower limit of 7.1$\times 10^{-22}$ eV, HIRES/MIKE returns a stronger limit of 14.3$\times 10^{-22}$ eV, while the combination of both data sets results in a limit of 20 $\times 10^{-22}$ eV (2$\sigma$ C.L.). The limits for the analysis of the combined data sets increases to 37.5$\times 10^{-22}$ eV (2$\sigma$ C.L.) when a smoother thermal history is assumed where the temperature of the IGM evolves as a power-law in redshift. Light boson masses in the range $1-10 \times10^{-22}$ eV are ruled out at high significance by our analysis, casting strong doubts that FDM helps solve the "small scale crisis" of the cold dark matter models.

Many models of dark matter include self-interactions beyond gravity. A variety of astrophysical observations have previously been used to place limits on the strength of such self-interactions. However, previous works have generally focused either on short-range interactions resulting in individual dark matter particles scattering from one another, or on effectively infinite-range interactions which sum over entire dark matter halos. In this work, we focus on the intermediate regime: forces with range much larger than dark matter particles' inter-particle spacing, but still shorter than the length scales of known halos. We show that gradients in the dark matter density of such halos would still lead to observable effects. We focus primarily on effects in the Bullet Cluster, where finite-range forces would lead either to a modification of the collision velocity of the cluster or to a separation of the dark matter and the galaxies of each cluster after the collision. We also consider constraints from the binding of ultrafaint dwarf galaxy halos, and from gravitational lensing of the Abell 370 cluster. Taken together, these observations allow us to set the strongest constraints on dark matter self-interactions over many orders of magnitude in range below $\sim10$ kpc, surpassing existing limits by orders of magnitude throughout.

support.quote: We constrain the abundance of primordial black holes (PBH) using 2622 microlensing events obtained from 5-years observations of stars in the Galactic bulge by the Optical Gravitational Lensing Experiment (OGLE). The majority of microlensing events display a single or at least continuous population that has a peak around the light curve timescale $t_{\rm E}\simeq 20~{\rm days}$ and a wide distribution over the range $t_{\rm E}\simeq [1, 300]~{\rm days}$, while the data also indicates a second population of 6 ultrashort-timescale events in $t_{\rm E}\simeq [0.1,0.3]~{\rm days}$, which are advocated to be due to free-floating planets. We confirm that the main population of OGLE events can be well modeled by microlensing due to brown dwarfs, main sequence stars and stellar remnants (white dwarfs and neutron stars) in the standard Galactic bulge and disk models for their spatial and velocity distributions. Using the dark matter (DM) model for the Milky Way (MW) halo relative to the Galactic bulge/disk models, we obtain the tightest upper bound on the PBH abundance in the mass range $M_{\rm PBH}\simeq[10^{-6},10^{-3}]M_\odot$ (Earth-Jupiter mass range), if we employ null hypothesis that the OGLE data does not contain any PBH microlensing event. More interestingly, we also show that Earth-mass PBHs can well reproduce the 6 ultrashort-timescale events, without the need of free-floating planets, if the mass fraction of PBH to DM is at a per cent level, which is consistent with other constraints such as the microlensing search for Andromeda galaxy (M31) and the longer timescale OGLE events. Our result gives a hint of PBH existence, and can be confirmed or falsified by microlensing search for stars in M31, because M31 is towards the MW halo direction and should therefore contain a much less number of free-floating planets, even if exist, than the direction to the MW center.

support.quote: We analyze the MeV/GeV emission from four bright Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRBs) observed by the Fermi-Large Area Telescope to produce robust, stringent constraints on a dependence of the speed of light in vacuo on the photon energy (vacuum dispersion), a form of Lorentz invariance violation (LIV) allowed by some Quantum Gravity (QG) theories. First, we use three different and complementary techniques to constrain the total degree of dispersion observed in the data. Additionally, using a maximally conservative set of assumptions on possible source-intrinsic spectral-evolution effects, we constrain any vacuum dispersion solely attributed to LIV. We then derive limits on the "QG energy scale" (the energy scale that LIV-inducing QG effects become important, E_QG) and the coefficients of the Standard Model Extension. For the subluminal case (where high energy photons propagate more slowly than lower energy photons) and without taking into account any source-intrinsic dispersion, our most stringent limits (at 95% CL) are obtained from GRB090510 and are E_{QG,1}>7.6 times the Planck energy (E_Pl) and E_{QG,2}>1.3 x 10^11 GeV for linear and quadratic leading order LIV-induced vacuum dispersion, respectively. These limits improve the latest constraints by Fermi and H.E.S.S. by a factor of ~2. Our results disfavor any class of models requiring E_{QG,1} \lesssim E_Pl.

support.quote: We report results of a search for nuclear recoils induced by weakly interacting massive particle (WIMP) dark matter using the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) two-phase xenon time projection chamber. This analysis uses a total exposure of $4.2\pm0.1$ tonne-years from 280 live days of LZ operation, of which $3.3\pm0.1$ tonne-years and 220 live days are new. A technique to actively tag background electronic recoils from $^{214}$Pb $\beta$ decays is featured for the first time. Enhanced electron-ion recombination is observed in two-neutrino double electron capture decays of $^{124}$Xe, representing a noteworthy new background. After removal of artificial signal-like events injected into the data set to mitigate analyzer bias, we find no evidence for an excess over expected backgrounds. World-leading constraints are placed on spin-independent (SI) and spin-dependent WIMP-nucleon cross sections for masses $\geq$9 GeV/$c^2$. The strongest SI exclusion set is $2.2\times10^{-48}$ cm$^{2}$ at the 90% confidence level and the best SI median sensitivity achieved is $5.1\times10^{-48}$ cm$^{2}$, both for a mass of 40 GeV/$c^2$.

canonical_record.label: Cupif-Giannini tree traversal
canonical_record.summary: NIST DADS describes Cupif-Giannini tree traversal as: Visit the leaves of a perfect binary tree with maximum dispersion: the next leaf has the maximum shortest-path distance from the preceding leaf, with less importance given to distance from earlier leaves. Use an n-bit counter for a tree of height n; successive bits choose left or right branches starting at the root. An initial random n-bit key can be XORed with the counter to permute the leaf-visit order.

support.quote:
Visit every
leaf
of a
perfect binary tree
with maximum dispersion (see note).  For a tree of
height
n, use an n-bit "count" integer.  The least significant bit of count indicates whether to go to the left or right
child
from the
root
. Each more significant bit indicates whether to go left or right.  Regular binary counting generates the list of 2
n
paths
to the leaves.
To randomly
permute
the order of leaf visits, choose a random n-bit "key" at the beginning. Use the
xor
of the key and the count to indicate which child to visit.

"Dispersion" means the next leaf visited is as far from other leaves visited as possible.  More formally, the next leaf has the maximum
shortest path
to the preceding leaf (with less importance given to be far from more distantly preceeding leaves).
It doesn't matter to the dispersion whether a 0 bit means left (and 1 means right) or 0 means right (and 1 means left).  Also the initial value of count doesn't matter, as long as overflow is handled.
To picture the algorithm, consider starting with a count of 000...00, indicating going down all left branches to the first leaf.  The next count is 000...01, which has a shortest path distance of 2n: from the first leaf, go up to the root, take the right branch, then down to the second leaf.  The next count is 000...10. This third leaf is 2n from the immediately preceding leaf (the second one) and 2n-1 from the first leaf: up to one below the root, then down to the first leaf.
Here is pseudocode for an inefficient Cupif-Giannini tree traversal with Xor "randomization" (** is the power operator, and ^ is xor):
visitNode(tree, nodeNumber, bitNumber)
begin
if isLeaf(tree), then
print(tree.root);
else
if the bitNumber-th bit of nodeNumber is 1, then
visitNode(tree.left_subtree, nodeNumber, bitNumber+1);
else
visitNode(tree.right_subtree, nodeNumber, bitNumber+1);
endif
endif
end
cupifGiannini(tree)
begin
key = random();
for n = 0 to 2**height(tree)-1
visitNode(tree, n ^ key, 1);
endfor
end

canonical_record.label: huge sparse array
canonical_record.summary: NIST DADS describes huge sparse array as: Store unique-key items using an item array large enough for the items and an uninitialized location array covering the much larger key range. Insertion records the next item position in the location array. Lookup validates the stored position against the number of inserted items and checks the item's key. Keys must be unique; duplicate keys require collision resolution. NIST reports linear total insertion and listing time, and constant lookup time, assuming constant-time allocation.

canonical_record.label: linear probing sort
canonical_record.summary: NIST DADS describes linear probing sort as: Distribute items into a larger array according to interpolation of their keys, putting collisions into the next empty location, then pack the items into an array of the original size. Note:
This is the upper-case Greek letter Omega.
This definition is stronger than the traditional mathematical definition.  Here, f must be greater than g FOR ALL x bigger than some k.  The traditional definition is f is big omega of g if it is not little o of g.  That is, one needs only an unbounded sequence of values of x tending to infinity such that cg(x) ≤ f(x) for all x in the sequence.
After Duncan Buell (
[email protected]
) 21 May 2004.

The problem of finding the shortest
path
in a
graph
from one
vertex
to another.  "Shortest" may be least number of
edges

Dijkstra's algorithm

DAG shortest paths
,
all pairs shortest path
,
single-source shortest-path problem
,
k
th
shortest path

Note:
The problem is to find the weight of the shortest path. For a map, it is to produce the (shortest) road distance from one city to another city, not which roads to take.
A modification to most algorithms finds the shortest path, too.  In
predecessor[i][j]
save the immediate predecessor of the shortest path from i to j.  Suppose predecessor[i][j] is k; then the shortest path ends with … → k → j.  If predecessor[i][k] is p, the shortest path ends with … → p → k → j.  Continue working backward until you reach i.

context_nodes.label: algorithm
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines algorithm as: A computable set of steps to achieve a desired result.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: algorithm

context_nodes.label: data structure
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines data structure as: An organization of information, usually in memory, for better algorithm efficiency , such as queue , stack , linked list , heap , dictionary , and tree , or conceptual unity, such as the name and address of a person. It may include redundant information, such as length of the list or number of nodes in a subtree .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: dataStructure

context_nodes.label: search
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines search as: Look for a value or item in a data structure. There are dozens of algorithms, data structures, and approaches.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: search

context_nodes.label: sort
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines sort as: Arrange items in a predetermined order. There are dozens of algorithms, the choice of which depends on factors such as the number of items relative to working memory, knowledge of the orderliness of the items or the range of the keys , the cost of comparing keys vs. the cost of moving items, etc. Most algorithms can be implemented as an in-place sort , and many can be implemented so they are stable , too. Formal Definition: The sort operation may be defined in terms of an initial array, S, of N items and a final array, S′, as follows. S′ i ≤ S′ i+1 , 0 < i < N (the items are in order) and S′ is a permutation of S.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: sort

context_nodes.label: binary search
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines binary search as: Search a sorted array by repeatedly dividing the search interval in half. Begin with an interval covering the whole array. If the value of the search key is less than the item in the middle of the interval, narrow the interval to the lower half. Otherwise narrow it to the upper half. Repeatedly check until the value is found or the interval is empty.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: binarySearch

context_nodes.label: linear search
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines linear search as: Search an array or list by checking items one at a time. Also known as sequential search.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: linearSearch

context_nodes.label: merge sort
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines merge sort as: A sort algorithm that splits the items to be sorted into two groups, recursively sorts each group, and merges them into a final, sorted sequence. Run time is Θ (n log n).

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: mergesort

context_nodes.label: quicksort
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines quicksort as: Pick an element from the array (the pivot), partition the remaining elements into those greater than and less than this pivot, and recursively sort the partitions. There are many variants of the basic scheme above: to select the pivot, to partition the array, to stop the recursion or switch to another algorithm for small partitions, etc.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: quicksort

context_nodes.label: heapsort
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines heapsort as: A sort algorithm that builds a heap , then repeatedly extracts the maximum item. Run time is O(n log n) .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: heapSort

context_nodes.label: insertion sort
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines insertion sort as: Sort by repeatedly taking the next item and inserting it into the final data structure in its proper order with respect to items already inserted. Run time is O(n 2 ) because of moves. Also known as linear insertion sort.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: insertionSort

context_nodes.label: selection sort
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines selection sort as: A sort algorithm that repeatedly searches remaining items to find the least one and moves it to its final location. The run time is Θ(n²) , where n is the number of elements. The number of swaps is O(n) .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: selectionSort

context_nodes.label: bubble sort
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines bubble sort as: Sort by comparing each adjacent pair of items in a list in turn, swapping the items if necessary, and repeating the pass through the list until no swaps are done. Also known as sinking sort, exchange sort.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bubblesort

context_nodes.label: counting sort
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines counting sort as: A 2-pass sort algorithm that is efficient when the number of distinct keys is small compared to the number of items. The first pass counts the occurrences of each key in an auxiliary array , and then makes a running total so each auxiliary entry is the number of preceding keys. The second pass puts each item in its final place according to the auxiliary entry for that key.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: countingsort

context_nodes.label: radix sort
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines radix sort as: A multiple pass distribution sort algorithm that distributes each item to a bucket according to part of the item's key beginning with the least significant part of the key. After each pass, items are collected from the buckets, keeping the items in order, then redistributed according to the next most significant part of the key.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: radixsort

context_nodes.label: bucket sort
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines bucket sort as: A distribution sort where input elements are initially distributed to several buckets based on an interpolation of the element's key . Each bucket is sorted if necessary, and the buckets' contents are concatenated. Also known as bin sort.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bucketsort

context_nodes.label: binary search tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines binary search tree as: A binary tree where every node's left subtree has keys less than the node's key, and every right subtree has keys greater than the node's key.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: binarySearchTree

context_nodes.label: AVL tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines AVL tree as: A balanced binary search tree where the height of the two subtrees ( children ) of a node differs by at most one. Look-up, insertion, and deletion are O(log n) , where n is the number of nodes in the tree.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: avltree

context_nodes.label: red-black tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines red-black tree as: A nearly-balanced tree that uses an extra bit per node to maintain balance. No leaf is more than twice as far from the root as any other. Formal Definition: A red-black tree with n internal nodes has height at most 2log 2 (n+1). Also known as symmetric binary B-tree.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: redblack

context_nodes.label: heap
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines heap as: A complete tree where every node has a key more extreme (greater or less) than or equal to the key of its parent . Usually understood to be a binary heap .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: heap

context_nodes.label: queue
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines queue as: A collection of items in which only the earliest added item may be accessed. Basic operations are add (to the tail ) or enqueue and delete (from the head ) or dequeue. Delete returns the item removed. Also known as "first-in, first-out" or FIFO. Formal Definition: It is convenient to define delete or dequeue in terms of remove and a new operation, front. The operations new(), add(v, Q), front(Q), and remove(Q) may be defined with axiomatic semantics as follows. new() returns a queue front(add(v, new())) = v remove(add(v, new())) = new() front(add(v, add(w, Q))) = front(add(w, Q)) remove(add(v, add(w, Q))) = add(v, remove(add(w, Q))) where Q is a queue and v and w are values. Also known as FIFO.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: queue

context_nodes.label: stack
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines stack as: A collection of items in which only the most recently added item may be removed. The latest added item is at the top. Basic operations are push and pop. Often top and isEmpty are available, too. Also known as "last-in, first-out" or LIFO. Formal Definition: The operations new(), push(v, S), top(S), and popoff(S) may be defined with axiomatic semantics as follows. new() returns a stack popoff(push(v, S)) = S top(push(v, S)) = v where S is a stack and v is a value. The pop operation is a combination of top, to return the top value, and popoff, to remove the top value. The predicate isEmpty(S) may be defined with the following additional axioms. isEmpty(new()) = true isEmpty(push(v, S)) = false Also known as LIFO.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: stack

context_nodes.label: linked list
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines linked list as: A list implemented by each item having a link to the next item. Also known as singly linked list.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: linkedList

context_nodes.label: doubly linked list
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines doubly linked list as: A variant of a linked list in which each item has a link to the previous item as well as the next. This allows easily accessing list items backward as well as forward and deleting any item in constant time. Also known as two-way linked list, symmetrically linked list.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: doublyLinkedList

context_nodes.label: graph
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines graph as: A set of items connected by edges . Each item is called a vertex or node . Formally, a graph is a set of vertices and a binary relation between vertices, adjacency. Formal Definition: A graph G can be defined as a pair (V,E), where V is a set of vertices, and E is a set of edges between the vertices E ⊆ {(u,v) | u, v ∈ V}. If the graph is undirected, the adjacency relation defined by the edges is symmetric , or E ⊆ {{u,v} | u, v ∈ V} (sets of vertices rather than ordered pairs). If the graph does not allow self-loops , adjacency is irreflexive .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: graph

context_nodes.label: Dijkstra's algorithm
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Dijkstra's algorithm as: An algorithm to find the shortest paths from a single source vertex to all other vertices in a weighted, directed graph . All weights must be nonnegative.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: dijkstraalgo

context_nodes.label: topological sort
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines topological sort as: To arrange items when some pairs of items have no comparison, that is, according to a partial order .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: topologicalSort

context_nodes.label: minimum spanning tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines minimum spanning tree as: A minimum-weight tree in a weighted graph which contains all of the graph's vertices . Also known as MST, shortest spanning tree, SST.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: minimumSpanningTree

context_nodes.label: Prim-Jarnik algorithm
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Prim-Jarnik algorithm as: Compute a minimum spanning tree by beginning with any vertex as the current tree . At each step add a least edge between any vertex not in the tree and any vertex in the tree. Continue until all vertices have been added.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: primJarnik

context_nodes.label: divide and conquer
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines divide and conquer as: Solve a problem, either directly because solving that instance is easy (typically, because the instance is small) or by dividing it into two or more smaller instances. Each of these smaller instances is recursively solved, and the solutions are combined to produce a solution for the original instance.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: divideAndConquer

context_nodes.label: trie
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines trie as: A tree for storing strings in which there is one node for every common prefix . The strings are stored in extra leaf nodes.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: trie

context_nodes.label: B-tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines B-tree as: A balanced search tree in which every node has between ⌈ m/2⌉ and m children , where m>1 is a fixed integer. m is the order . The root may have as few as 2 children. This is a good structure if much of the tree is in slow memory (disk), since the height , and hence the number of accesses, can be kept small, say one or two, by picking a large m. Also known as balanced multiway tree.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: btree

context_nodes.label: finite state machine
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines finite state machine as: A model of computation consisting of a set of states , a start state , an input alphabet , and a transition function that maps input symbols and current states to a next state . Computation begins in the start state with an input string. It changes to new states depending on the transition function. There are many variants, for instance, machines having actions (outputs) associated with transitions ( Mealy machine ) or states ( Moore machine ), multiple start states, transitions conditioned on no input symbol (a null) or more than one transition for a given symbol and state ( nondeterministic finite state machine ), one or more states designated as accepting states ( recognizer ), etc. Also known as finite state automaton.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: finiteStateMachine

context_nodes.label: balanced binary tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines balanced binary tree as: A binary tree where no leaf is more than a certain amount farther from the root than any other. After inserting or deleting a node , the tree may rebalanced with rotations .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: balancedbitr

context_nodes.label: priority queue
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines priority queue as: An abstract data type to efficiently support finding the item with the highest priority across a series of operations. The basic operations are: insert, find-minimum (or maximum), and delete-minimum (or maximum). Some implementations also efficiently support join two priority queues ( meld ), delete an arbitrary item, and increase the priority of a item (decrease-key). Formal Definition: The operations new(), insert(v, PQ), find-minimum or min(PQ), and delete-minimum or dm(PQ) may be defined with axiomatic semantics as follows. new() returns a priority queue min(insert(v, new())) = v dm(insert(v, new())) = new() min(insert(v, insert(w, PQ))) = if priority(v) < priority(min(insert(w, PQ))) then v else min(insert(w, PQ)) dm(insert(v, insert(w, PQ))) = if priority(v) < priority(min(insert(w, PQ))) then insert(w, PQ) else insert(v, dm(insert(w, PQ))) where PQ is a priority queue, v and w are items, and priority(v) is the priority of item v.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: priorityque

context_nodes.label: hash table
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines hash table as: A dictionary in which keys are mapped to array positions by hash functions . Having the keys of more than one item map to the same position is called a collision . There are many collision resolution schemes , but they may be divided into open addressing , chaining , and keeping one special overflow area. Perfect hashing avoids collisions, but may be time-consuming to create. Also known as scatter storage.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: hashtab

context_nodes.label: breadth-first search
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines breadth-first search as: Any search algorithm that considers neighbors of a vertex , that is, outgoing edges of the vertex's predecessor in the search, before any outgoing edges of the vertex. Extremes are searched last. This is typically implemented with a queue .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: breadthfirst

context_nodes.label: depth-first search
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines depth-first search as: (1) Any search algorithm that considers outgoing edges ( children ) of a vertex before any of the vertex's siblings , that is, outgoing edges of the vertex's predecessor in the search. Extremes are searched first. This is easily implemented with recursion . (2) An algorithm that marks all vertices in a directed graph in the order they are discovered and finished, partitioning the graph into a forest . Also known as DFS.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: depthfirst

context_nodes.label: Kruskal's algorithm
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Kruskal's algorithm as: An algorithm for computing a minimum spanning tree . It maintains a set of partial minimum spanning trees, and repeatedly adds the shortest edge in the graph whose vertices are in different partial minimum spanning trees.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: kruskalsalgo

context_nodes.label: greedy algorithm
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines greedy algorithm as: An algorithm that always takes the best immediate, or local, solution while finding an answer. Greedy algorithms find the overall, or globally, optimal solution for some optimization problems , but may find less-than-optimal solutions for some instances of other problems.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: greedyalgo

context_nodes.label: binary tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines binary tree as: A tree with at most two children for each node . Formal Definition: A binary tree either is empty (no nodes), or has a root node, a left binary tree, and a right binary tree. Also known as dyadic tree.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: binarytree

context_nodes.label: directed graph
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines directed graph as: A graph whose edges are ordered pairs of vertices . That is, each edge can be followed from one vertex to another vertex. Formal Definition: A graph G is a pair (V,E), where V is a set of vertices, and E is a set of edges between the vertices E ⊆ {(u,v) | u, v ∈ V}. If the graph does not allow self-loops , adjacency is irreflexive , that is E ⊆ {(u,v) | u, v ∈ V ∧ u ≠ v}. Also known as digraph, oriented graph.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: directedGraph

context_nodes.label: deterministic finite state machine
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines deterministic finite state machine as: A finite state machine with at most one transition for each symbol and state . Also known as DFA, deterministic finite automaton.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: determFinitStateMach

context_nodes.label: nondeterministic finite state machine
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines nondeterministic finite state machine as: A finite state machine whose transition function maps inputs symbols and states to a (possibly empty) set of next states . The transition function also may map the null symbol (no input symbol needed) and states to next states. Also known as NFA, nondeterministic finite automaton.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: nondetermFiniteStateMach

context_nodes.label: array
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines array as: An assemblage of items that are randomly accessible by integers, the index. Formal Definition: Ignoring size an array may be seen as an abstract data type with the operations new(), set(i, v, A), and get(i, A), where i is a numeric index, v is a value, and A is an array. The operations may be defined with axiomatic semantics as follows. new() returns an array get(i, set(i, v, A)) = v get(i, set(j, v, A)) = get(i, A) if i ≠ j Compare this with a dictionary using integers as keys. If the contents of a new array are set to some implicit initial value v i , we could add the following rule for get. get(i, new()) = v i Typically arrays have a fixed size and use either 0-based indexing or 1-based indexing . Fixed initial size and 0-based indexing may incorporated as follows. new(s) returns an array, which has a size s size(new(s)) = s size(set(i, v, A)) = size(A) get(i, set(i, v, A)) = v if 0 ≤ i < size(A) get(i, set(j, v, A)) = get(i, A) if i ≠ j One-based or other indexing may be defined similarly.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: array

context_nodes.label: list
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines list as: A collection of items accessible one after another beginning at the head and ending at the tail .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: list

context_nodes.label: set
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines set as: An unordered collection of values where each value occurs at most once. A group of elements with three properties: (1) all elements belong to a universe , (2) either each element is a member of the set or it is not, and (3) the elements are unordered. Formal Definition: As an abstract data type , a set has a single query function, isIn(v, S), which tells whether an element is a member of the set or not, and two modifier functions, add(v, S) and remove(v, S). These may be defined with axiomatic semantics as follows. new() returns a set isIn(v, new()) = false isIn(v, add(v, S)) = true isIn(v, add(u, S)) = isIn(v , S) if v ≠ u remove(v, new()) = new() remove(v, add(v, S)) = remove(v, S) remove(v, add(u, S)) = add(u, remove(v, S)) if v ≠ u where S is a set and u and v are elements. The predicate isEmpty(S) may be defined with the following additional axioms. isEmpty(new()) = true isEmpty(add(v, S)) = false

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: set

context_nodes.label: tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines tree as: (1) A data structure accessed beginning at the root node. Each node is either a leaf or an internal node . An internal node has one or more child nodes and is called the parent of its child nodes. All children of the same node are siblings . Contrary to a physical tree, the root is usually depicted at the top of the structure, and the leaves are depicted at the bottom. (2) A connected , undirected , acyclic graph . It is rooted and ordered unless otherwise specified. Thanks to Joshua O'Madadhain ( [email protected] ) for the figure, 6 October 2005. Formal Definition: (1) A tree is either empty (no nodes), or a root and zero or more subtrees. The subtrees are ordered.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: tree

context_nodes.label: vertex
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines vertex as: An item in a graph . Sometimes referred to as a node .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: vertex

context_nodes.label: path
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines path as: A list of vertices of a graph where each vertex has an edge between it and the next vertex.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: path

context_nodes.label: cycle
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines cycle as: A path that starts and ends at the same vertex and includes at least one edge .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: cycle

context_nodes.label: weighted graph
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines weighted graph as: A graph having a weight, or number, associated with each edge . Some algorithms require all weights to be nonnegative, integral, positive, etc. Also known as edge-weighted graph.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: weightedGraph

context_nodes.label: connected graph
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines connected graph as: An undirected graph that has a path between every pair of vertices .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: connectedGraph

context_nodes.label: complete graph
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines complete graph as: An undirected graph with an edge between every pair of vertices .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: completeGraph

context_nodes.label: bipartite graph
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines bipartite graph as: An undirected graph where vertices can be partition ed into two sets such that no edge connects vertices in the same set.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bipartgraph

context_nodes.label: directed acyclic graph
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines directed acyclic graph as: A directed graph with no path that starts and ends at the same vertex . Also known as DAG, acyclic directed graph, oriented acyclic graph.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: directAcycGraph

context_nodes.label: abstract data type
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines abstract data type as: A set of data values and associated operations that are precisely specified independent of any particular implementation. Also known as ADT.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: abstractDataType

context_nodes.label: circular list
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines circular list as: A variant of a linked list in which the nominal tail is linked to the head . The entire list may be accessed starting at any item and following links until one comes to the starting item again.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: circularlist

context_nodes.label: binary heap
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines binary heap as: A complete binary tree where every node has a key more extreme (greater or less) than or equal to the key of its parent .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: binaryheap

context_nodes.label: splay tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines splay tree as: A binary search tree in which operations that access nodes restructure the tree.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: splaytree

context_nodes.label: 2-3 tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines 2-3 tree as: A B-tree of order 3, that is, internal nodes have two or three children .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: two3tree

context_nodes.label: suffix tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines suffix tree as: A compact representation of a trie corresponding to the suffixes of a given string where all nodes with one child are merged with their parents .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: suffixtree

context_nodes.label: suffix array
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines suffix array as: An array of all starting positions of suffixes of a string arranged in lexicographical order . This allows a binary search or fast substring search.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: suffixarray

context_nodes.label: hash function
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines hash function as: A function that maps keys to integers, usually to get an even distribution on a smaller set of values. Also known as hash.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: hash

context_nodes.label: perfect hashing
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines perfect hashing as: A hash function that maps each different key to a distinct integer. Usually all possible keys must be known beforehand. A hash table that uses a perfect hash has no collisions . Formal Definition: A function f is perfect for a set of keys K iff ∀ j, k ∈ K f(j) = f(k) → j = k. Also known as optimal hashing.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: perfecthash

context_nodes.label: open addressing
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines open addressing as: A class of collision resolution schemes in which all items are stored within the hash table . In case of collision , other positions are computed, giving a probe sequence , and checked until an empty position is found. Some ways of computing possible new positions are less efficient because of clustering . Typically items never move once put in place, but in Robin Hood hashing , LCFS hashing , and other techniques, previously placed items may move.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: openAddressing

context_nodes.label: cuckoo hashing
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines cuckoo hashing as: A dictionary implemented with two hash tables , T 1 and T 2 , and two different hash functions , h 1 and h 2 . Each key , k, is either in T 1 [h 1 (k)] or T 2 [h 2 (k)]. A new key , k, is stored in T 1 [h 1 (k)]. If that location is already occupied by another key, l, the other key is moved to T 2 [h 2 (l)]. Keys are moved back and forth until a key moves to an empty location or a limit is reached. If the limit is reached, new hash functions are chosen, and the tables are rehashed. For tables that are a bit less than half full and with carefully chosen universal hashing functions, performance is good. A key is deleted by removing it from a table.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: cuckooHashing

context_nodes.label: recursion
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines recursion as: An algorithmic technique where a function, in order to accomplish a task, calls itself with some part of the task.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: recursion

context_nodes.label: exhaustive search
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines exhaustive search as: An algorithm that finds a solution by trying every possibility.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: exhaustiveSearch

context_nodes.label: jump search
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines jump search as: Search a sorted array by checking every j th item until the right area is found, then doing a linear search . The optimum for n items is when j=√ n. Also known as block search.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: jumpsearch

context_nodes.label: Huffman coding
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Huffman coding as: A minimal variable-length character coding based on the frequency of each character. First, each character becomes a one-node binary tree , with the character as the only node . The character's frequency is the tree's frequency. Two trees with the least frequencies are joined as the subtrees of a new root that is assigned the sum of their frequencies. Repeat until all characters are in one tree. One code bit represents each level . Thus more frequent characters are near the root and are coded with few bits, and rare characters are far from the root and are coded with many bits. Also known as static Huffman coding.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: huffmanCoding

context_nodes.label: string matching
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines string matching as: The problem of finding occurrence(s) of a pattern string within another string or body of text. There are many different algorithms for efficient searching. Also known as exact string matching, string searching, text searching.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: stringMatching

context_nodes.label: Shell sort
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Shell sort as: The first diminishing increment sort . On each pass i sets of n/i items are sorted, typically with insertion sort . On each succeeding pass, i is reduced until it is 1 for the last pass. A good series of i values is important to efficiency.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: shellsort

context_nodes.label: comb sort
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines comb sort as: An in-place sort algorithm that repeatedly reorders different pairs of items. On each pass swap pairs of items separated by the increment or gap, if needed, and reduce the gap (divide it by about 1.3). The gap starts at about 3/4 of the number of items. Continue until the gap is 1 and a pass had no swaps.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: combSort

context_nodes.label: gnome sort
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines gnome sort as: Put items in order by comparing the current item with the previous item. If they are in order, move to the next item (or stop if the end is reached). If they are out of order, swap them and move to the previous item. If there is no previous item, move to the next item.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: gnomeSort

context_nodes.label: in-place sort
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines in-place sort as: A sort algorithm in which the sorted items occupy the same storage as the original ones. These algorithms may use o(n) additional memory for bookkeeping, but at most a constant number of items are kept in auxiliary memory at any time. Also known as sort in place.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: inplacesort

context_nodes.label: external sort
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines external sort as: Any sort algorithm that uses external memory, such as tape or disk, during the sort. Since most common sort algorithms assume high-speed random access to all intermediate memory, they are unsuitable if the values to be sorted don't fit in main memory.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: externalsort

context_nodes.label: bitonic sort
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines bitonic sort as: Compare, and swap if necessary, pairs of elements in parallel. Subsets are sorted then merged. Also known as Batcher sort.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bitonicSort

context_nodes.label: finite state transducer
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines finite state transducer as: A finite state machine specifically with a read-only input and a write-only output. The input and output cannot be reread or changed.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: finiteStateTransducer

context_nodes.label: big-O notation
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines big-O notation as: A theoretical measure of the execution of an algorithm , usually the time or memory needed, given the problem size n, which is usually the number of items. Informally, saying some equation f(n) = O(g(n)) means it is less than some constant multiple of g(n). The notation is read, "f of n is big oh of g of n". Formal Definition: f(n) = O(g(n)) means there are positive constants c and k, such that 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ cg(n) for all n ≥ k. The values of c and k must be fixed for the function f and must not depend on n. Also known as O, asymptotic upper bound.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bigOnotation

context_nodes.label: NP-complete
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines NP-complete as: The complexity class of decision problems for which answers can be checked for correctness, given a certificate , by an algorithm whose run time is polynomial in the size of the input (that is, it is NP ) and no other NP problem is more than a polynomial factor harder. Informally, a problem is NP-complete if answers can be verified quickly, and a quick algorithm to solve this problem can be used to solve all other NP problems quickly.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: npcomplete

context_nodes.label: polynomial time
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines polynomial time as: When the execution time of a computation, m(n), is no more than a polynomial function of the problem size, n. More formally m(n) = O(n k ) where k is a constant.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: polynomialtm

context_nodes.label: Bond Sequential Search
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Bond Sequential Search as: Search an array or list for two keys at once by using the bitwise or of the keys as the search key. When a possible match is found, compare each key against the item.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: BondSeqSearch

context_nodes.label: Commentz-Walter
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Commentz-Walter as: A multiple string matching algorithm that compares from the end of the pattern , like Boyer-Moore , using a finite state machine , like Aho-Corasick .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: CommentzWalter

context_nodes.label: JSort
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines JSort as: An in-place sort that partially orders the array twice with build-heap , once moving lesser items earlier and once in reverse moving greater items later, then uses insertion sort on the nearly-ordered array.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: JSort

context_nodes.label: Merkle tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Merkle tree as: A tree (usually a binary tree ) in which each internal node has a hash of all the information in the leaf nodes under it. Specifically, each internal node has a hash of the information in its children . Each leaf has a hash of the block of information it represents. All leaf nodes are at the same depth . All nodes are as far left as possible. To add a block (leaf) to a full tree, a new root is created with the old root as its left child. Its right child is a degenerate tree (only left subtrees) all the way to the leaf level. Also known as hash tree.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: MerkleTree

context_nodes.label: SSTable
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines SSTable as: An immutable dictionary stored on disk. Values are far larger than keys. Keys and values are in key-order in a "data block". Ordered keys are in an "index block", where each key has an offset into its location in the data block. Also known as sorted-string table.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: SSTable

context_nodes.label: (a,b)-tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines (a,b)-tree as: A search tree with the restrictions that all leaves are at the same depth and all internal nodes have between a and b children , where a and b are integers such that 2 ≤ a ≤ (b+1)/2. The root may have as few as 2 children.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: abtree

context_nodes.label: acyclic graph
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines acyclic graph as: A graph with no path that starts and ends at the same vertex .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: acyclicgraph

context_nodes.label: adaptive heap sort
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines adaptive heap sort as: A variant of heapsort that uses a randomized binary search tree (RBST) to structure the input according to any preexisting order. The RBST is used to select candidates that are put into the heap so the heap doesn't need to keep track of all elements.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: adaptiveHeapSort

context_nodes.label: adaptive Huffman coding
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines adaptive Huffman coding as: A near-minimal variable-length character coding that changes based on the frequency of characters processed. As characters are processed, frequencies are updated and codes are changed (or, the coding tree is modified). Also known as dynamic Huffman coding.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: adaptiveHuffman

context_nodes.label: adjacent
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines adjacent as: Two vertices of a graph are adjacent if there is an edge between them. Two edges of a graph are adjacent if they connect the same vertex.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: adjacent

context_nodes.label: algorithm FGK
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines algorithm FGK as: An adaptive Huffman coding scheme. Coding is never much worse than twice optimal .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: algorithmFGK

context_nodes.label: alternating path
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines alternating path as: A path with alternating free and matched edges.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: alterntngpth

context_nodes.label: American flag sort
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines American flag sort as: An efficient, in-place variant of radix sort that distributes items into hundreds of buckets . The first step counts the number of items in each bucket, and the second step computes where each bucket will start in the array. The last step cyclically permutes items to their proper bucket. Since the buckets are in order in the array, there is no collection step. The name comes by analogy with the Dutch national flag problem in the last step: efficiently partition the array into many "stripes". Using some efficiency techniques, it is twice as fast as quicksort for large sets of strings.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: americanFlagSort

context_nodes.label: approximation algorithm
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines approximation algorithm as: An algorithm to solve an optimization problem that runs in polynomial time in the length of the input and outputs a solution that is guaranteed to be close to the optimal solution . "Close" has some well-defined sense called the performance guarantee .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: approximatin

context_nodes.label: arborescence
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines arborescence as: Informally, a directed tree .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: arborescence

context_nodes.label: bag
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines bag as: An unordered collection of values that may have duplicates. Formal Definition: A bag has a single query function, numberIn(v, B), which tells how many copies of an element are in the bag, and two modifier functions, add(v, B) and remove(v, B). These may be defined with axiomatic semantics as follows. new() returns a bag numberIn(v, new()) = 0 numberIn(v, add(v, B)) = 1 + numberIn(v, B) numberIn(v, add(u, B)) = numberIn(v, B) if v ≠ u remove(v, new()) = new() remove(v, add(v, B)) = B remove(v, add(u, B)) = add(u, remove(v, B)) if v ≠ u where B is a bag and u and v are elements. The predicate isEmpty(B) may be defined with the following additional axioms. isEmpty(new()) = true isEmpty(add(v, B)) = false Also known as multi-set.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bag

context_nodes.label: balanced two-way merge sort
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines balanced two-way merge sort as: A balanced k-way merge sort that sorts a data stream using repeated merges. It distributes the input into two streams by repeatedly reading a block of input that fits in memory, a run , sorting it, then writing it to the next stream. It then repeatedly merges the two streams and puts each merged run into one of two output streams until there is a single sorted output.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: balancedqsrt

context_nodes.label: balanced tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines balanced tree as: A tree where no leaf is much farther away from the root than any other leaf. Different balancing schemes allow different definitions of "much farther" and different amounts of work to keep them balanced.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: balancedtree

context_nodes.label: balanced k-way merge sort
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines balanced k-way merge sort as: A merge sort that sorts a data stream using repeated merges. It distributes the input into k streams by repeatedly reading a block of input that fits in memory, called a run , sorting it, then writing it to the next stream. It then repeatedly merges the k streams and puts each merged run into one of j output streams until there is a single sorted output.

context_nodes.label: BB(α) tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines BB(α) tree as: A binary tree where the balance of every subtree, ρ(T'), is bounded by α ≤ ρ(T') ≤ 1-α. Also known as weight-balanced tree.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bbalphatree

context_nodes.label: BD-tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines BD-tree as: A binary tree that organizes multidimensional points by splitting off regular subintervals.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bdtree

context_nodes.label: biconnected graph
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines biconnected graph as: A connected graph that is not broken into disconnected pieces by deleting any single vertex (and incident edges ).

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: biconnectedGraph

context_nodes.label: bidirectional bubble sort
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines bidirectional bubble sort as: A variant of bubble sort that compares each adjacent pair of items in a list in turn, swapping them if necessary, and alternately passes through the list from the beginning to the end then from the end to the beginning. It stops when a pass does no swaps. Also known as cocktail shaker sort, shaker sort, double-direction bubble sort.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bidirectionalBubbleSort

context_nodes.label: binary priority queue
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines binary priority queue as: A priority queue implemented with a binary tree having the following restrictions: The key of a node is greater than keys of its children , i.e., it has the heap property . If the right subtree is not empty, the left subtree is not empty. If there are both left and right children, the left child's key is greater than the right child's key.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: binaryPriorityQueue

context_nodes.label: binary relation
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines binary relation as: A relation between exactly two items at a time, such as "greater than" (>), "not equal to" (≠), "proper subset of" (⊂), or "is connected to" (has an edge to) for vertices of a graph .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: binaryRelation

context_nodes.label: binary function
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines binary function as: A function with two arguments.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: binaryfunc

context_nodes.label: binary insertion sort
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines binary insertion sort as: Insertion sort in which the proper location for the next item is found with a binary search .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: binaryinsort

context_nodes.label: bingo sort
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines bingo sort as: A variant of selection sort that orders items by first finding the least value, then repeatedly moving all items with that value to their final location and find the least value for the next pass. This is more efficient than selection sort if there are many duplicate values.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bingosort

context_nodes.label: blind sort
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines blind sort as: A specialized sort algorithm that first builds a blind trie , then traverse the tree left to right.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: blindSort

context_nodes.label: block addressing index
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines block addressing index as: An inverted index that includes the block , or general location, within texts, in addition to the text in which the word appears.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: blockAddressingIndex

context_nodes.label: boolean function
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines boolean function as: A function whose range is {0, 1}. It can be understood to evaluate the truth or falsity of each element of its domain .

context_nodes.label: bounded queue
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines bounded queue as: A queue limited to a fixed number of items.

context_nodes.label: bounded stack
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines bounded stack as: A stack limited to a fixed number of items.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: boundedstack

context_nodes.label: BPP
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines BPP as: The class of languages for which a membership computation by a probabilistic Turing machine halts in polynomial time with the right answer (accept or reject) at least 2/3 of the time. "BPP" means " B ounded error P robability in P olynomial" time. Also known as bounded error probability in polynomial time.

context_nodes.label: British Museum technique
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines British Museum technique as: Find a solution by checking all possibilities one by one, beginning with the smallest. This is a conceptual, not a practical, technique where the number of possibilities are enormous.

context_nodes.label: brute force string search with mismatches
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines brute force string search with mismatches as: Beginning with the (leftmost) position in a string and trying each position in turn, find the number of characters for which the pattern and the substring beginning at that position don't match (the Hamming distance ). Return the first position with k or fewer mismatches.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bruteForceStrSrchwMismatch

context_nodes.label: brute force string search
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines brute force string search as: Find a string in another string or body of text by trying each position one at a time. There are many far faster string matching algorithms. Also known as naive string search.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bruteForceStringSearch

context_nodes.label: brute force
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines brute force as: An algorithm that inefficiently solves a problem, often by trying every one of a wide range of possible solutions.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bruteforce

context_nodes.label: BSP-tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines BSP-tree as: A binary space partitioning (BSP) tree is a binary tree for multidimensional points where successive levels are split by arbitrary hyperplanes.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bsptree

context_nodes.label: B*-tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines B*-tree as: A B-tree in which nodes are kept 2/3 full by redistributing keys to fill two child nodes, then splitting them into three nodes.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bstartree

context_nodes.label: bucket
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines bucket as: An area of storage where items with a common property are stored. Typically tree data structures and sort algorithms use many buckets, one for each group of items. Usually buckets are kept on disk.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bucket

context_nodes.label: bucket trie
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines bucket trie as: A variant of a trie in which leaf nodes are buckets which hold up to k strings. Usually implies fixed sized buckets.

context_nodes.label: buddy tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines buddy tree as: A point access method which splits multidimensional space in different dimensions at each level. It also keeps a minimum bounding box of points accessible by each node.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: buddytree

context_nodes.label: cactus stack
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines cactus stack as: A variant of stack in which one other cactus stack may be attached to the top. An attached stack is called a "branch." When a branch becomes empty, it is removed. Pop is not allowed if there is a branch. A branch is only accessible through the original reference; it is not accessible through the stack. Formal Definition: The operations new to this variant of stack, branch(S, T) and notch(v), may be defined with axiomatic semantics as follows. top(branch(S, T)) = top(S) notch(new()) = false notch(push(v, S)) = false notch(branch(S, T)) = true Also known as saguaro stack.

context_nodes.label: canonical complexity class
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines canonical complexity class as: One of the classes defined by logarithmic , polynomial , and exponential bounds on time and space, for deterministic and nondeterministic machines. These classify most of the important computational problems.

context_nodes.label: Caverphone
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Caverphone as: An algorithm to code English names phonetically.

context_nodes.label: cell tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines cell tree as: A spatial access method where successive levels are split by arbitrary hyperplanes. Concave objects are decomposed into convex pieces. Each convex piece is indexed in every cell which it overlaps.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: celltree

context_nodes.label: chaining
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines chaining as: A class of collision resolution schemes in which linked lists handle collisions in a hash table . The two main subclasses are separate chaining , where lists are outside the table, and coalesced chaining , where the lists are within the table.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: chaining

context_nodes.label: clique
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines clique as: A set of vertices in an undirected graph in which there is an edge between every pair of vertices. In other words, a subgraph that is complete .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: clique

context_nodes.label: coalesced chaining
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines coalesced chaining as: A scheme in which linked lists within the hash table handle collisions . An item that collides is put in the next empty place in the array and added to the end of a list embedded in the array items. Any open addressing method to compute possible new positions may be used to find the "next" empty place.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: coalescedChaining

context_nodes.label: coding tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines coding tree as: A full binary tree that represents a coding, such as produced by Huffman coding . Each leaf is an encoded symbol. The path from the root to a leaf is its codeword.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: codingTree

context_nodes.label: collective recursion
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines collective recursion as: A special form of tail recursion , where the results are produced during the recursive calls and nothing is returned. The recursion may be optimized away by executing the call in the current stack frame, rather than creating a new stack frame, or by deallocating the entire recursion stack at once rather than a little at each return.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: collectiveRecursion

context_nodes.label: collision resolution scheme
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines collision resolution scheme as: A way of handling collisions , that is, when two or more items should be kept in the same location, especially in a hash table . The general ways are keeping subsequent items within the table and computing possible locations ( open addressing ), keeping lists for items that collide ( chaining ), or keeping one special overflow area.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: collisionres

context_nodes.label: compact data structure
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines compact data structure as: A data structure that needs far less space and allows efficient access without decompression.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: compactDataStruct

context_nodes.label: compact trie
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines compact trie as: A trie in which nonbranching subtrees leading to leaf nodes are cut off.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: compactTrie

context_nodes.label: complete binary tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines complete binary tree as: A binary tree in which every level (depth), except possibly the deepest, is completely filled. At depth n, the height of the tree, all nodes must be as far left as possible.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: completeBinaryTree

context_nodes.label: complete tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines complete tree as: A tree in which every level , except possibly the deepest, is entirely filled. At depth n, the height of the tree, all nodes are as far left as possible.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: completetree

context_nodes.label: complexity class
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines complexity class as: Any of a set of computational problems with the same bounds ( Θ(n) ) on time and space, for deterministic and nondeterministic machines.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: complexityClass

context_nodes.label: compound algorithm
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines compound algorithm as: An algorithm in which one or more of the computable steps is a call to execute another algorithm.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: compoundAlgorithm

context_nodes.label: concurrent data structure
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines concurrent data structure as: A data structure designed to work correctly while being accessed by many asynchronous threads. The two main types are blocking and nonblocking.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: concurrentDataStructure

context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines confluently persistent data structure as: A fully persistent data structure that allows meld or merge operations to combine two different versions.

context_nodes.label: constant function
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines constant function as: A function that always gives the same value.

context_nodes.label: cut vertex
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines cut vertex as: A vertex whose deletion along with incident edges results in a graph with more components than the original graph. Also known as articulation point.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: cutvertex

context_nodes.label: dense graph
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines dense graph as: A graph in which the number of edges is close to the possible number of edges.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: densegraph

context_nodes.label: derangement
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines derangement as: A permutation of elements, where no element is in its original position.
