context_nodes.label: deterministic algorithm
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines deterministic algorithm as: An algorithm whose behavior can be completely predicted from the input.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: deterministicAlgorithm

context_nodes.label: Deutsch-Jozsa algorithm
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Deutsch-Jozsa algorithm as: A quantum algorithm to determine whether a function is constant or balanced, that is, returns 1 for half the domain and 0 for the other half. For a function taking n input qubits, first, do Hadamards on n 0's, forming all possible inputs, and a single 1, which will be the answer qubit. Next, run the function once; this exclusive or 's the result with the answer qubit. Finally, do Hadamards on the n inputs again, and measure the answer qubit. If it is 0, the function is constant, otherwise the function is balanced.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: deutschJozsaAlgo

context_nodes.label: dichotomic search
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines dichotomic search as: Search by selecting between two distinct alternatives (dichotomies) at each step.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: dichotomicSearch

context_nodes.label: dictionary
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines dictionary as: An abstract data type storing items, or values. A value is accessed by an associated key . Basic operations are new, insert, find and delete. Formal Definition: The operations new(), insert(k, v, D), and find(k, D) may be defined with axiomatic semantics as follows. new() returns a dictionary find(k, insert(k, v, D)) = v find(k, insert(j, v, D)) = find(k, D) if k ≠ j where k and j are keys, v is a value, and D is a dictionary. The modifier function delete(k, D) may be defined as follows. delete(k, new()) = new() delete(k, insert(k, v, D)) = delete(k, D) delete(k, insert(j, v, D)) = insert(j, v, delete(k, D)) if k ≠ j If we want find to be a total function , we could define find(k, new()) using a special value: fail . This only changes the return type of find. find(k, new()) = fail Also known as association list, map, property list.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: dictionary

context_nodes.label: digital search tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines digital search tree as: A trie which stores the strings in internal nodes , so there is no need for extra leaf nodes to store the strings.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: digitalSearchTree

context_nodes.label: digital tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines digital tree as: A tree for storing strings in which nodes are organized by substrings common to two or more strings.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: digitaltree

context_nodes.label: diminishing increment sort
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines diminishing increment sort as: An in-place sort algorithm that repeatedly reorders different, small subsets of the input until the entire array is ordered. On each pass it handles i sets of n/i items, where n is the total number of items. Each set is every i th item, e.g. set 1 is item 1, 1+i, 1+2i, etc., set 2 is item 2, 2+i, etc. On each succeeding pass, the increment or gap, i, is reduced until it is 1 for the last pass.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: diminishingIncSort

context_nodes.label: direct chaining
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines direct chaining as: A collision resolution scheme in which the hash table is an array of links to lists . Each list holds all the items with the same hash value.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: directChaining

context_nodes.label: discrete interval encoding tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines discrete interval encoding tree as: A binary search tree that stores consecutive values as intervals. Also known as diet.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: discretintrv

context_nodes.label: distribution sort
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines distribution sort as: Any sort algorithm where items are distributed from the input to multiple intermediate structures, which are then gathered and placed on the output.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: distributionSort

context_nodes.label: distributive partitioning sort
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines distributive partitioning sort as: Step 1: find the median key . Step 2: distribute the n items into n/2 buckets linearly covering the interval from the minimum to the median and n/2 buckets linearly covering the interval from the median to the maximum. Step 3: compact the buckets, removing empty buckets. Recursively start again at step 1 for any bucket with multiple items. Linked lists are used to avoid moving items until a final phase and to avoid bucket overflows.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: distributivePartitioningSort

context_nodes.label: double metaphone

It returns two codes if a word has two plausible pronunciations, such as a foreign word. This reduces matching problems from wrong spelling.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: doubleMetaphone

context_nodes.label: dual
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines dual as: The dual of a planar graph , G, is a graph with a vertex for each region in G and an edge between vertices for each pair of adjacent regions. The new edge crosses the edge in G which is the boundary between the adjacent regions.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: dual

context_nodes.label: dual-pivot quicksort
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines dual-pivot quicksort as: Pick two elements from the array to be sorted (the pivots), partition the remaining elements into (i) those less than the lesser pivot, (ii) those between the pivots, and (iii) those greater than the greater pivot, and recursively sort these partitions.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: dualPivotQuicksort

context_nodes.label: dynamic hashing
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines dynamic hashing as: A hash table that grows to handle more items. The associated hash function must change as the table grows. Some schemes may shrink the table to save space when items are deleted.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: dynamicHashing

context_nodes.label: dynamic array
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines dynamic array as: An array whose size may change over time. Items are not only added or removed, but memory used changes, too.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: dynamicarray

context_nodes.label: easy split, hard merge
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines easy split, hard merge as: A recursive algorithm, especially a sort algorithm, where dividing (splitting) into smaller problems is quick or simple and combining (merging) the solutions is time consuming or complex.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: easySplitHardMerge

context_nodes.label: 8 queens
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines 8 queens as: Place eight chess queens on an 8 × 8 board such that no queen can attack another. Efficiently find all possible placements.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: elasticBucketTrie

context_nodes.label: Euclidean Steiner tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Euclidean Steiner tree as: A tree of minimum Euclidean distance connecting a set of points, called terminals , in the plane. This tree may include points other than the terminals, which are called Steiner points .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: euclidSteinerTree

context_nodes.label: Euler cycle
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Euler cycle as: A path through a graph which starts and ends at the same vertex and includes every edge exactly once. Also known as Eulerian path, Königsberg bridges problem.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: eulercycle

context_nodes.label: EXCELL
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines EXCELL as: A point access method using a dynamic multidimensional array .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: excell

context_nodes.label: extended binary tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines extended binary tree as: A binary tree with special nodes replacing every null subtree. Every regular node has two children , and every special node has no children.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: extendedBinaryTree

context_nodes.label: extendible hashing
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines extendible hashing as: A hash table in which the hash function is the last few bits of the key and the table refers to buckets . Table entries with the same final bits may use the same bucket. If a bucket overflows, it splits, and if only one entry referred to it, the table doubles in size. If a bucket is emptied by deletion, entries using it are changed to refer to an adjoining bucket, and the table may be halved.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: extendibleHashing

context_nodes.label: extended k-d tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines extended k-d tree as: A spatial access method where successive levels are split along different dimensions into nonoverlapping cells. Objects are indexed in all cells they intersect.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: extendkdtree

context_nodes.label: external quicksort
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines external quicksort as: Read the M/2 first and last elements into a buffer (the buffer acts like the pivot in quicksort ), and sort them. Read the next element from the beginning or end to balance writing. If the next element is less than the least of the buffer, write it to available space at the beginning. If greater than the greatest, write it to the end. Otherwise write the greatest or least of the buffer, and put the next element in the buffer. Keep the maximum lower and minimum upper keys written to avoid resorting middle elements that are in order. When done, write the buffer. Recursively sort the smaller partition, and loop to sort the remaining partition.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: externalQuicksort

context_nodes.label: Fibonacci tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Fibonacci tree as: A variant of a binary tree where a tree of order n (n>1) has a left subtree of order n-1 and a right subtree of order n-2. An order 0 Fibonacci tree has no nodes , and an order 1 tree has 1 node.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: fibonacciTree

context_nodes.label: free vertex
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines free vertex as: A vertex not on a matched edge in a matching , or, one which has not been matched.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: freevertex

context_nodes.label: full binary tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines full binary tree as: A binary tree in which each node has exactly zero or two children . Also known as proper binary tree.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: fullBinaryTree

context_nodes.label: full inverted index
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines full inverted index as: An inverted index that includes the exact location within texts, in addition to the text in which the word appears.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: fullInvertedIndex

context_nodes.label: fully persistent data structure
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines fully persistent data structure as: A persistent data structure that allows updates to all versions, previous and latest.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: fullyPersistData

context_nodes.label: function
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines function as: (1) A computation which takes some arguments or inputs and yields an output. Any particular input yields the same output every time. More formally, a mapping from each element in the domain to an element in the range . (2) A subroutine which returns a value.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: function

context_nodes.label: GBD-tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines GBD-tree as: A generalized BD-tree , hence the name, which stores spatially extended objects as a hierarchy of minimum bounding boxes . It is a balanced multiway tree which serves as a spatial access method .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: gbdtree

context_nodes.label: grid file
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines grid file as: A point access method which splits space into a nonperiodic grid. Each spatial dimension is divided by a linear hash . Small sets of points are referred to by one or more cells of the grid.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: gridfile

context_nodes.label: halting problem
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines halting problem as: Is there an algorithm to determine whether any arbitrary program halts? Turing proved the answer is, no. Since many questions can be recast to this problem, we can conclude that some programs are absolutely impossible, although heuristic or partial solutions are possible.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: haltingProblem

context_nodes.label: Hamiltonian cycle
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Hamiltonian cycle as: A path through a graph that starts and ends at the same vertex and includes every other vertex exactly once. Also known as tour.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: hamiltonianCycle

context_nodes.label: Hamiltonian path
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Hamiltonian path as: A simple path through a graph that includes every vertex in the graph.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: hamiltonianPath

context_nodes.label: hard split, easy merge
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines hard split, easy merge as: A recursive algorithm, especially a sort algorithm, where dividing (splitting) into smaller problems is time consuming or complex and combining (merging) the solutions is quick or trivial.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: hardSplitEasyMerge

context_nodes.label: hashbelt
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines hashbelt as: Use a short list or array of hash tables to implement a hash table with aging to expire items. To expire items, add a new table at the head of the list and drop the oldest table, along with its contents. To find an item, search all the tables.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: hashbelt

context_nodes.label: hB-tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines hB-tree as: A point access method which uses k-d trees to organize the space, but partitions as excluded intervals, like the BANG file . Searching is like in a k-d-B-tree .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: hbtree

context_nodes.label: heap property
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines heap property as: Each node in a tree has a key which is more extreme (greater or less) than or equal to the key of its parent .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: heapproperty

context_nodes.label: height-balanced binary search tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines height-balanced binary search tree as: A height-balanced tree which is also a binary search tree . It supports membership, insert, and delete operations in time logarithmic in the number of nodes in the tree.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: heightBalancedBinSrchTree

context_nodes.label: height-balanced tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines height-balanced tree as: A tree whose subtrees differ in height by no more than one and the subtrees are height-balanced, too. An empty tree is height-balanced.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: heightBalancedTree

context_nodes.label: heuristic
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines heuristic as: An algorithm that usually, but not always, works or that gives nearly the right answer.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: heuristic

context_nodes.label: histogram sort
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines histogram sort as: An efficient 3-pass refinement of a bucket sort algorithm. The first pass counts the number of items for each bucket in an auxiliary array , and then makes a running total so each auxiliary entry is the number of preceding items. The second pass puts each item in its proper bucket according to the auxiliary entry for the key of that item. The last pass sorts each bucket. Also known as interpolation sort.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: histogramSort

context_nodes.label: ideal random shuffle
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines ideal random shuffle as: A permutation algorithm, or shuffle, that has exactly the same chance of producing any permutation.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: idealRandomShuffle

context_nodes.label: in-order traversal
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines in-order traversal as: Process all nodes of a tree by recursively processing the left subtree, then processing the root , and finally the right subtree. Also known as symmetric traversal.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: inorderTraversal

context_nodes.label: introspective sort
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines introspective sort as: A variant of quicksort which switches to heapsort for pathological inputs, that is, when execution time is becoming quadratic. Also known as introsort.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: introspectiveSort

context_nodes.label: inverse suffix array
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines inverse suffix array as: For each position in a string , the inverse suffix array has its index in the string's suffix array . Formal Definition: Given a suffix array, sa, and the corresponding inverse suffix array, isa, isa[i] = j iff sa[j] = i.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: inverseSuffixArray

context_nodes.label: inversion list
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines inversion list as: A set of non-overlapping numeric ranges, stored in an array in increasing order. Items in odd indexes begin ranges, and items in even indexes are the first number after the ends. Use a form of binary search to determine if a number is in any of the ranges. If the search ends on an odd index (a beginning), the number is in the set. If the search ends on an even index (a just-after-end) or outside the array, it is not in the set.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: inversionList

context_nodes.label: inverted file index
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines inverted file index as: An inverted index that only indicates the text in which a word appears, not where the word appears within the text.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: invertedFileIndex

context_nodes.label: inverted index
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines inverted index as: An index into a set of texts of the words in the texts. The index is accessed by some search method. Each index entry gives the word and a list of texts, possibly with locations within the text, where the word occurs.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: invertedIndex

context_nodes.label: J sort
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines J sort as: An in-place sort algorithm that uses strand sort to sort fewer than about 40 items and shuffle sort to sort more.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: j_sort

context_nodes.label: Johnson-Trotter
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Johnson-Trotter as: Generate permutations by swapping one adjacent pair of elements at a time. Also known as Steinhaus-Johnson-Trotter, Trotter-Johnson.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: johnsonTrotter

context_nodes.label: k²-tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines k²-tree as: A compact representation of a sparse directed graph . It requires 1 to 3 bits per edge. Many access functions, like successor(s), predecessor(s), and range (all links from a range of vertices to another range of vertices), have very efficient implementations.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: k2tree

context_nodes.label: k-ary tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines k-ary tree as: A tree with no more than k children for each node . Also known as k-way tree.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: karyTree

context_nodes.label: k-ary heap
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines k-ary heap as: A complete tree where every node has a key more extreme (greater or less) than the key of its parent . Each node has k or fewer children .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: karyheap

context_nodes.label: k-d tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines k-d tree as: A multidimensional search tree for points in k dimensional space. Levels of the tree are split along successive dimensions at the points.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: kdtree

context_nodes.label: Kripke structure
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Kripke structure as: A nondeterministic finite state machine whose states are labeled with boolean variables, which are the evaluations of expressions in that state. It may be extended with fairness constraints.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: kripkeStruct

context_nodes.label: k-way merge sort
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines k-way merge sort as: A merge sort that sorts a data stream using repeated merges. It distributes the input into k streams by repeatedly reading a block of input that fits in memory, called a run , sorting it, then writing it to the next stream. It merges runs from the k streams into an output stream. It then repeatedly distributes the runs in the output stream to the k streams and merges them until there is a single sorted output. Also known as p-way merge sort.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: kwayMergeSort

context_nodes.label: labeled graph
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines labeled graph as: A graph which has labels associated with each edge or each vertex .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: labeledgraph

context_nodes.label: Las Vegas algorithm
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Las Vegas algorithm as: A randomized algorithm that always produces correct results, with the only variation from one run to another being its running time.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: lasVegas

context_nodes.label: leftist tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines leftist tree as: A priority queue implemented with a variant of a binary tree . Every node has a count which is the distance to the nearest leaf . In addition to the heap property , leftist trees are kept so the right descendant of each node has the shorter distance to a leaf.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: leftisttree

context_nodes.label: level-order traversal
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines level-order traversal as: Process all nodes of a tree by depth : first the root , then the children of the root, etc. Equivalent to a breadth-first search from the root.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: levelOrderTraversal

context_nodes.label: linear hash
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines linear hash as: A numeric function that maintains the order of input keys while changing their spacing. Formal Definition: A hash function f for keys in S such that k1, k2 ∈ S ∧ k1 > k2 → f(k1) > f(k2). Also known as order-preserving hash.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: linearhash

context_nodes.label: little-o notation
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines little-o notation as: A theoretical measure of the execution of an algorithm , usually the time or memory needed, given the problem size n, which is usually the number of items. Informally, saying some equation f(n) = o(g(n)) means f(n) becomes insignificant relative to g(n) as n approaches infinity. The notation is read, "f of n is little oh of g of n". Formal Definition: f(n) = o(g(n)) means for all c > 0 there exists some k > 0 such that 0 ≤ f(n) < cg(n) for all n ≥ k. The value of k must not depend on n, but may depend on c.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: littleOnotation

context_nodes.label: locality-sensitive hashing
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines locality-sensitive hashing as: A probabilistic algorithm to quickly find points in a high dimensional space near a query point. Preprocessing: put every point in multiple hash tables . Each table has its own locality-sensitive hash function and uses buckets (or chaining ) since many collisions are expected. The hash functions come from a family of functions. Finding: look up the query point in each hash table, and compute the distance from the query point of every point in the bucket.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: localitySensitiveHashing

context_nodes.label: lower triangular matrix
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines lower triangular matrix as: A matrix that is only defined at (i,j) when i ≥ j.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: lowerTriangularMatrix

context_nodes.label: Markov chain
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Markov chain as: A finite state machine with probabilities for each transition, that is, a probability that the next state is s j given that the current state is s i .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: markovchain

context_nodes.label: matched vertex
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines matched vertex as: A vertex on an matched edge in a matching , or, one which has been matched.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: matchedvertx

context_nodes.label: matrix
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines matrix as: A two-dimensional array. By convention, the first index is the row, and the second index is the column.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: matrix

context_nodes.label: max-heap property
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines max-heap property as: Each node in a tree has a key which is less than or equal to the key of its parent .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: maxheapprop

context_nodes.label: Mealy machine
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Mealy machine as: A finite state machine which produces an output for each transition .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: mealyMachine

context_nodes.label: metaphone
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines metaphone as: An algorithm to code English words phonetically by reducing them to 16 consonant sounds. A better variant is double metaphone .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: metaphone

context_nodes.label: min-heap property
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines min-heap property as: Each node in a tree has a key which is greater than or equal to the key of its parent .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: minheapprop

context_nodes.label: minimal perfect hashing
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines minimal perfect hashing as: A perfect hashing function that maps each different key to a distinct integer and has the same number of possible integers as keys. Formal Definition: A function f is a minimal perfect hash function for a set of keys K iff ∀ j, k ∈ K f(j) = f(k) → j = k and the range of f(k) is 1… |K|.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: minimalPerfectHash

context_nodes.label: model of computation
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines model of computation as: A formal, abstract definition of a computer. Using a model one can more easily analyze the intrinsic execution time or memory space of an algorithm while ignoring many implementation issues. There are many models of computation which differ in computing power (that is, some models can perform computations impossible for other models) and the cost of various operations.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: modelOfComputation

context_nodes.label: Monte Carlo algorithm
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Monte Carlo algorithm as: A randomized algorithm that may produce incorrect results, but with bounded error probability.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: monteCarlo

context_nodes.label: Moore machine
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Moore machine as: A finite state machine that produces an output for each state .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: mooreMachine

context_nodes.label: move-to-front heuristic
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines move-to-front heuristic as: A heuristic that moves the target of a search to the head of a list so it is found faster next time.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: movefront

context_nodes.label: multi suffix tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines multi suffix tree as: A suffix tree extended to multiple strings by concatenating the strings .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: multiSuffixTree

context_nodes.label: multikey Quicksort
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines multikey Quicksort as: Pick an element from the array (the pivot). Consider the first character (key) of the string (multikey). Partition the remaining elements into three sets: those whose corresponding character is less than, equal to, and greater than the pivot's character. Recursively sort the "less than" and "greater than" partitions on the same character. Recursively sort the "equal to" partition by the next character (key). Also known as three-way radix quicksort.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: multikeyQuicksort

context_nodes.label: multilayer grid file
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines multilayer grid file as: A spatial access method which is two or more simultaneous grid files . Objects reside in the first grid file where it doesn't have to be split across hyperplanes.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: multilaygrd

context_nodes.label: multiway tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines multiway tree as: A tree with any number of children for each node .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: multiwaytree

context_nodes.label: n-ary function
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines n-ary function as: (1) A function with exactly n arguments. (2) A function which takes any number of arguments, or a variable number of arguments.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: naryfunc

context_nodes.label: nondeterministic algorithm
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines nondeterministic algorithm as: A conceptual algorithm with more than one allowed step at certain times and which always takes the right or best step. It is not random, as in randomized algorithm , or indeterminate. Rather it has the supercomputational characteristic of choosing the optimal behavior.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: nondetermAlgo

context_nodes.label: NP
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines NP as: The complexity class of decision problems for which answers can be checked by an algorithm whose run time is polynomial in the size of the input. Note that this doesn't require or imply that an answer can be found quickly, only that any claimed solution can be verified quickly. "NP" is the class that a N ondeterministic Turing machine accepts in P olynomial time. Also known as nondeterministic polynomial time.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: np

context_nodes.label: NP-hard
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines NP-hard as: The complexity class of decision problems that are intrinsically harder than those that can be solved by a nondeterministic Turing machine in polynomial time . When a decision version of a combinatorial optimization problem is proved to belong to the class of NP-complete problems, then the optimization version is NP-hard.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: nphard

context_nodes.label: n queens
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines n queens as: Place n chess queens on an n × n board such that no queen can attack another. Efficiently find all possible placements.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: nqueens

context_nodes.label: NYSIIS
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines NYSIIS as: Convert a name to a phonetic coding of up to six characters.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: nysiis

context_nodes.label: oblivious algorithm
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines oblivious algorithm as: An algorithm whose behavior, by design, is independent of some property that influences a typical algorithm for the same problem.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: obliviousAlgorithm

context_nodes.label: off-line algorithm
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines off-line algorithm as: An algorithm which is given the entire sequence of inputs in advance.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: offline

context_nodes.label: on-line algorithm
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines on-line algorithm as: An algorithm that must process each input in turn, without detailed knowledge of future inputs.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: online

context_nodes.label: optimal polyphase merge sort
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines optimal polyphase merge sort as: An external sort algorithm that uses optimal polyphase merges .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: optimalPolyphaseMergeSort

context_nodes.label: optimization problem
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines optimization problem as: A computational problem in which the object is to find the best of all possible solutions. More formally, find a solution in the feasible region which has the minimum (or maximum) value of the objective function .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: optimization

context_nodes.label: order-preserving minimal perfect hashing
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines order-preserving minimal perfect hashing as: A minimal perfect hashing function for keys in S such that if k1, k2 ∈ S and k1 > k2, then f(k1) > f(k2).

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: orderPreservMinPerfectHash

context_nodes.label: ordered linked list
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines ordered linked list as: A linked list whose items are kept in some order.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: orderedLinkedList

context_nodes.label: oscillating merge sort
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines oscillating merge sort as: Given n tape drives, one input and n-1 work drives, distribute a portion of the input to n-2 tapes, then merge them onto the final tape reading the n-2 backward. Repeat until n-2 (backward) merged runs have been created, at which time they are merged. Continue building up powers of n-2 batches until done.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: oscillatingMergeSort

context_nodes.label: P
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines P as: The complexity class of languages that can be accepted by a deterministic Turing machine in polynomial time .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: p

context_nodes.label: pagoda
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines pagoda as: A priority queue implemented with a variant of a binary tree . The root points to its children, as in a binary tree. Every other node points back to its parent and down to its leftmost (if it is a right child ) or rightmost (if it is a left child) descendant leaf . The basic operation is merge or meld , which maintains the heap property . An element is inserted by merging it as a singleton. The root is removed by merging its right and left children. Merging is bottom-up, merging the leftmost edge of one with the rightmost edge of the other.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: pagoda

context_nodes.label: partially persistent data structure
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines partially persistent data structure as: A persistent data structure that allows updates to the latest version only.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: partiallyPersistData

context_nodes.label: Pearson's hash
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Pearson's hash as: A hash function that uses an auxiliary array, but no shift or exclusive-or ( xor ) operations.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: pearsonshash

context_nodes.label: perfect binary tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines perfect binary tree as: A binary tree with all leaf nodes at the same depth . All internal nodes have degree 2.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: perfectBinaryTree

context_nodes.label: perfect shuffle
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines perfect shuffle as: Split a list of elements (or deck of cards) exactly in half then precisely interleave the two halves.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: perfectShuffle

context_nodes.label: permutation
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines permutation as: A rearrangement of elements, where none are lost, added, or changed. The Fisher-Yates shuffle randomly permutes elements. Also known as shuffle.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: permutation

context_nodes.label: persistent data structure
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines persistent data structure as: A data structure that preserves its old versions, that is, previous versions may be queried in addition to the latest version.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: persistentDataStructure

context_nodes.label: phonetic coding
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines phonetic coding as: Code a string based on how it is pronounced.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: phoneticCoding

context_nodes.label: pigeonhole sort
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines pigeonhole sort as: A 2-pass sort algorithm that is efficient when the range of keys is approximately equal to the number of items. The first pass allocates an array of buckets , one bucket for each possible key value, then moves each item to its key's bucket. The second pass goes over the bucket array moving each item to the next place in the destination.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: pigeonholeSort

context_nodes.label: planar graph
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines planar graph as: A graph that can be drawn in the plane with no crossing edges .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: planargraph

context_nodes.label: planar straight-line graph
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines planar straight-line graph as: A graph that can be embedded in the plane without crossings in which every edge in the graph is a straight line segment. It is sometimes referred to as planar subdivision or map.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: planarstrght

context_nodes.label: point access method
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines point access method as: A data structure and associated algorithms primarily to search for points defined in multidimensional space. Also known as PAM.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: pointAccessMethod

context_nodes.label: polyphase merge sort
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines polyphase merge sort as: A merge sort algorithm that reduces the number of intermediate files needed by reusing emptied files.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: polyphmrgsrt

context_nodes.label: polytope
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines polytope as: A closed, bounded N-dimensional figure whose faces are hyperplanes. Informally, a multidimensional solid with flat sides. A generalization of polyhedron.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: polytope

context_nodes.label: postman's sort
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines postman's sort as: A highly engineered variant of top-down radix sort where attributes of the key are described so the algorithm can allocate buckets and distribute efficiently.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: postmansort

context_nodes.label: postorder traversal
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines postorder traversal as: Process all nodes of a tree by recursively processing all subtrees, then finally processing the root . Also known as postfix traversal.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: postorderTraversal

context_nodes.label: Post's correspondence problem
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Post's correspondence problem as: Given a set of pairs of strings , find a sequence of pairs such that the concatenation of all first members of the pairs is the same string as the concatenation of all second members. This is an undecidable problem . Also known as PCP.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: postsCorrespondProb

context_nodes.label: preorder traversal
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines preorder traversal as: Process all nodes of a tree by processing the root , then recursively processing all subtrees. Also known as prefix traversal.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: preorderTraversal

context_nodes.label: primitive algorithm
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines primitive algorithm as: An algorithm in which all the computable steps are basic operations.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: primitiveAlgorithm

context_nodes.label: probabilistic algorithm
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines probabilistic algorithm as: Any algorithm that works for all practical purposes but has a theoretical chance of being wrong.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: probablAlgo

context_nodes.label: proper subset
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines proper subset as: A set S 2 is a proper subset of another set S 1 if every element in S 2 is in S 1 and S 1 has some elements which are not in S 2 .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: propersubset

context_nodes.label: P-tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines P-tree as: (1) A spatial access method that defines hyperplanes, in addition to the orthogonal dimensions, which node boundaries may parallel. Space is split by hierarchically nested polytopes (multidimensional boxes with nonrectangular sides). The R-tree is a special case that has no additional hyperplanes. (2) A spatial access method that splits space by hierarchically nested polytopes. The R-tree is a special case in which all polytopes are boxes.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: ptree

context_nodes.label: q sort
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines q sort as: The sort function in many libraries. It is generally a combination of quicksort, for many items, and insertion sort , for a few items.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: qsort

context_nodes.label: quantum computation
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines quantum computation as: Computation based on quantum mechanical effects, such as superposition and entanglement, in addition to classical digital manipulations.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: quantumComputation

context_nodes.label: ragged matrix
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines ragged matrix as: A matrix having irregular numbers of items in each row.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: raggedmatrix

context_nodes.label: random search
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines random search as: Repeatedly check items in an array at random until successful.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: randomSearch

context_nodes.label: randomized algorithm
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines randomized algorithm as: An algorithm that makes random (or pseudorandom) choices.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: randomizedAlgo

context_nodes.label: randomized binary search tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines randomized binary search tree as: A binary search tree in which nodes have a randomly assigned priority. Updates keep priorities in heap order instead of keeping balance information and doing rebalance operations. Also known as cartesian tree, RBST.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: randomizedBinarySearchTree

context_nodes.label: range sort
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines range sort as: A bucket sort where the function to determine the bucket is based on the range of possible keys .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rangesort

context_nodes.label: rapid sort
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines rapid sort as: A 2-pass sort algorithm that is efficient when the range of keys is approximately equal to the number of items and only keys are sorted. The first pass counts the occurrences of each key in an auxiliary array . The second pass goes over the auxiliary array writing the counted number of keys to the destination.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rapidSort

context_nodes.label: rectangular matrix
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines rectangular matrix as: An n × m matrix , or, one whose size may not be the same in both dimensions.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rectangmatrx

context_nodes.label: rectilinear Steiner tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines rectilinear Steiner tree as: A minimum-length rectilinear tree connecting a set of points, called terminals , in the plane. This tree may include points other than the terminals, which are called Steiner points .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rectilinearSteinertree

context_nodes.label: recursive data structure
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines recursive data structure as: A data structure that is partially composed of smaller or simpler instances of the same data structure. For instance, a tree is composed of smaller trees ( subtrees ) and leaf nodes , and a list may have other lists as elements.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: recursivstrc

context_nodes.label: relation
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines relation as: A computation which takes some inputs and yields an output. Any particular input may yield different outputs at different times. Formally, a mapping from each element in the domain to one or more elements in the range .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: relation

context_nodes.label: reservoir sampling
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines reservoir sampling as: Randomly select k items from a stream of items of unknown length. Save the first k items in an array of size k. For each item j, j > k, choose a random integer M from 1 to j (inclusive). If M ≤ k, replace item M of the array with item j.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: reservoirSampling

context_nodes.label: restricted universe sort
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines restricted universe sort as: A sort algorithm that operates on the basis that the keys are members of a restricted set of values. They may not require comparisons of keys to perform the sorting.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: restricted

context_nodes.label: R-file
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines R-file as: A spatial access method which divides space into a hierarchically of nested boxes. Objects are indexed in the lowest cell which completely contains them.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rfile

context_nodes.label: ρ-approximation algorithm
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines ρ-approximation algorithm as: An approximation algorithm guaranteed to find a solution at most (or at least, as appropriate) ρ times the optimum. The ratio ρ is the performance ratio or relative performance guarantee of the algorithm.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rhoapproxmtn

context_nodes.label: search tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines search tree as: A tree where every subtree of a node has keys less than any other subtree of the node to its right. The keys in a node are conceptually between subtrees and are greater than any keys in subtrees to its left and less than any keys in subtrees to its right.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: searchtree

context_nodes.label: self-organizing list
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines self-organizing list as: A list that reorders the elements based on some self-organizing heuristic [Wikipedia] to improve average access time.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: selfOrganizingList

context_nodes.label: separate chaining
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines separate chaining as: A scheme in which each position in the hash table has a list to handle collisions . Each position may be just a link to the list ( direct chaining ) or may be an item and a link, essentially, the head of a list. In the latter, one item is in the table, and other colliding items are in the list. Also known as external chaining.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: separateChaining

context_nodes.label: shuffle sort
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines shuffle sort as: A distribution sort algorithm that begins by removing the first 1/8 of the n items, sorting them (recursively), and putting them in an array. This creates n/8 buckets to which the remaining 7/8 of the items are distributed. Each bucket is then sorted, and the buckets are concatenated.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: shuffleSort

context_nodes.label: simple path
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines simple path as: A path that repeats no vertex , except that the first and last may be the same vertex.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: simplepath

context_nodes.label: simplex
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines simplex as: The simplest N-dimensional polytope . The generalization of a triangle (2D) or tetrahedron (3D).

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: simplex

context_nodes.label: skd-tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines skd-tree as: The spatial k-d tree is a spatial access method where successive levels are split along different dimensions. Objects are indexed by their centroid , and the minimum bounding box of objects in a node are stored in the node.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: skdtree

context_nodes.label: skip list
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines skip list as: A randomized variant of an ordered linked list with additional, parallel lists. Parallel lists at higher levels skip geometrically more items. Searching begins at the highest level, to quickly get to the right part of the list, then uses progressively lower level lists. A new item is added by randomly selecting a level, then inserting it in order in the lists for that and all lower levels. With enough levels, searching is O(log n) .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: skiplist

context_nodes.label: smoothsort
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines smoothsort as: A variant of heapsort that takes advantage of a partially ordered table. Performance is O(n) when input is sorted and O(n log n) performance for worst case .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: smoothsort

context_nodes.label: sorted array
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines sorted array as: An array whose items are kept sorted, often so searching is faster.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: sortedarray

context_nodes.label: sorted list
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines sorted list as: A list whose items are kept sorted.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: sortedlist

context_nodes.label: soundex
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines soundex as: An algorithm to code surnames phonetically by reducing them to the first letter and up to three digits, where each digit is one of six consonant sounds. This reduces matching problems from different spellings.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: soundex

context_nodes.label: spanning tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines spanning tree as: A connected , acyclic subgraph containing all the vertices of a graph .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: spanningtree

context_nodes.label: sparse graph
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines sparse graph as: A graph in which the number of edges is much less than the possible number of edges.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: sparsegraph

context_nodes.label: sparse matrix
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines sparse matrix as: A matrix that has relatively few non-zero (or "interesting") entries. It may be represented in much less than n × m space.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: sparsematrix

context_nodes.label: spatial access method
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines spatial access method as: A data structure to search for lines, polygons, etc. Also known as SAM.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: spatialAccessMethod

context_nodes.label: square matrix
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines square matrix as: A n × n matrix , i.e., one whose size is the same in both dimensions.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: squarematrix

context_nodes.label: stable
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines stable as: An algorithm where the relative order upon input of items with equal keys is always preserved in the output. Usually a sort algorithm.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: stable

context_nodes.label: state machine
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines state machine as: A model of computation consisting of a (possibly infinite) set of states , a set of start states , an input alphabet , and a transition function which maps input symbols and current states to a next state . Usually understood to be a finite state machine .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: statemachine

context_nodes.label: Steiner tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Steiner tree as: A minimum-weight tree connecting a designated set of vertices , called terminals , in an undirected , weighted graph or points in a space. The tree may include non-terminals, which are called Steiner vertices or Steiner points .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: steinertree

context_nodes.label: Steiner vertex
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Steiner vertex as: A point that is not part of the input set of points, for instance, a point computed to construct a Steiner tree .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: steinervertx

context_nodes.label: strand sort
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines strand sort as: A sort algorithm that works well if many items are in order. First, begin a sublist by moving the first item from the original list to the sublist. For each subsequent item in the original list, if it is greater than the last item of the sublist, remove it from the original list and append it to the sublist. Merge the sublist into a final, sorted list. Repeatedly extract and merge sublists until all items are sorted. Handle two or fewer items as special cases.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: strandSort

context_nodes.label: strictly lower triangular matrix
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines strictly lower triangular matrix as: A matrix that is only defined at (i,j) when i > j.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: strictlyLowerTriangMat

context_nodes.label: strictly upper triangular matrix
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines strictly upper triangular matrix as: A matrix that is only defined at (i,j) when i < j.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: strictlyUpperTriangMat

context_nodes.label: string matching with errors
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines string matching with errors as: Searching for approximate (e.g., up to a predefined number of symbol mismatches, insertions, and deletions) occurrences of a pattern string in a text string. Preprocessing, e.g., building an index, may or may not be allowed. Also known as approximate string matching.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: stringMatchwError

context_nodes.label: string matching with mismatches
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines string matching with mismatches as: The special case of string matching with errors where mismatches are the only type of error allowed.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: stringMatchwMismatch

context_nodes.label: strip packing
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines strip packing as: Pack a set of rectangles into a strip of width 1 to minimize the height used. Rectangles may not overlap or be rotated. Without loss of generality, the height of rectangles is at most 1. This is NP-hard .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: strippacking

context_nodes.label: strongly connected component
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines strongly connected component as: A strongly connected subgraph , S, of a directed graph , D, such that no vertex of D can be added to S and it still be strongly connected. Informally, a maximal subgraph in which every vertex is reachable from every other vertex.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: stronglyConnectedCompo

context_nodes.label: strongly connected graph
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines strongly connected graph as: A directed graph that has a path from each vertex to every other vertex. Formal Definition: A directed graph D=(V, E) such that for all pairs of vertices u, v ∈ V, there is a path from u to v and from v to u.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: stronglyConnectedGraph

context_nodes.label: strongly NP-hard
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines strongly NP-hard as: The complexity class of decision problems which are still NP-hard even when all numbers in the input are bounded by some polynomial in the length of the input.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: stronglyNP

context_nodes.label: sublinear time algorithm
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines sublinear time algorithm as: A algorithm whose execution time, f(n), grows slower than the size of the problem, n, but only gives an approximate or probably correct answer.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: sublinearTimeAlgo

context_nodes.label: subset
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines subset as: A set S 1 is a subset of another set S 2 if every element in S 1 is in S 2 . S 2 may have exactly the same elements as S 1 . Formal Definition: S 1 ⊆ S 2 iff ∀ s, s ∈ S 1 → s ∈ S 2 .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: subset

context_nodes.label: tail recursion
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines tail recursion as: A special form of recursion where the last operation of a function is a recursive call. The recursion may be optimized away by executing the call in the current stack frame and returning its result rather than creating a new stack frame.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: tailRecursion

context_nodes.label: ternary search tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines ternary search tree as: A 3-way tree where every node's left subtree has keys less than the node's key, every middle subtree has keys equal to the node's key, and every right subtree has keys greater than the node's key. If the key is a multikey ( string , array, list, etc.), the middle subtree organizes by the next subkey (character, array or list item, etc.) Also known as TST.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: ternarySearchTree

context_nodes.label: threaded tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines threaded tree as: A binary search tree in which each node uses an otherwise-empty left child link to refer to the node's in-order predecessor and an empty right child link to refer to its in-order successor.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: threadedtree

context_nodes.label: top-down radix sort
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines top-down radix sort as: A recursive bucket sort where elements are distributed based on succeeding pieces (characters) of the key .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: topdownRadixSort

context_nodes.label: total function
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines total function as: A function which is defined for all inputs of the right type, that is, for all of a domain .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: totalfunc

context_nodes.label: transpose sequential search
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines transpose sequential search as: Search an array or list by checking items one at a time. If the value is found, swap it with its predecessor so it is found faster next time. Also known as self-organizing sequential search.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: transposeSeqSearch

context_nodes.label: traveling salesman
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines traveling salesman as: Find a path through a weighted graph that starts and ends at the same vertex , includes every other vertex exactly once, and minimizes the total cost of edges . Also known as TSP.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: travelingSalesman

context_nodes.label: treap
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines treap as: A binary search tree in which nodes have another key , called the priority. Operations also keep the nodes heap ordered with regard to the priority.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: treap

context_nodes.label: tree traversal
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines tree traversal as: A technique for processing the nodes of a tree in some order.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: treeTraversal

context_nodes.label: treesort (1)
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines treesort (1) as: A sort algorithm that first builds a binary search tree of the keys , then accesses the keys with an in-order traversal .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: treesort1

context_nodes.label: treesort (2)
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines treesort (2) as: Variants of heapsort .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: treesort2

context_nodes.label: trinary function
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines trinary function as: A function with three arguments.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: trinaryfunc

context_nodes.label: twin grid file
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines twin grid file as: A point access method which is two simultaneous grid files . Points are shuffled between the primary and secondary file to minimize the total size.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: twingridfl

context_nodes.label: 2-3-4 tree
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines 2-3-4 tree as: A B-tree of order 4, that is, internal nodes have two, three, or four children .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: two34tree

context_nodes.label: Two Way algorithm
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Two Way algorithm as: Partition ("factor") the pattern , x, into left, x l , and right, x r , parts in such a way to optimize searching. Compare x r left to right then, if it matches, compare x l right to left.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: twoWay

context_nodes.label: two-level grid file
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines two-level grid file as: A point access method which is two levels of grid files . The first level addresses second level grid files.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: twolevgrid

context_nodes.label: unary function
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines unary function as: A function which takes one argument.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: unaryfunc

context_nodes.label: unbiased coin flipping algorithm
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines unbiased coin flipping algorithm as: To get unbiased random bits, flip a coin twice. If it comes up heads then tails, the result bit is 1. It it comes up tails then heads, the result is 0. Repeat the double flips until one of these occurs.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: unbiasedCoinFlipAlgo

context_nodes.label: undecidable problem
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines undecidable problem as: A problem that cannot be solved for all cases by any algorithm whatsoever---equivalently, whose associated language cannot be recognized by a Turing machine that halts for all inputs.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: undecidableProblem

context_nodes.label: undirected graph
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines undirected graph as: A graph whose edges are unordered pairs of vertices . That is, each edge connects two vertices. Formal Definition: A graph G is a pair (V,E), where V is a set of vertices, and E is a set of edges between the vertices E ⊆ {{u,v} | u, v ∈ V}. If the graph does not allow self-loops , adjacency is irreflexive , that is E ⊆ {{u,v} | u, v ∈ V ∧ u ≠ v}.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: undirectedGraph

context_nodes.label: uniform matrix
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines uniform matrix as: A matrix having the same number of items in each row.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: uniformmatrx

context_nodes.label: UnShuffle sort
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines UnShuffle sort as: A distribution sort with two phases. In the first phase, the inputs are distributed among doubly-ended queues keeping the items in each queue ordered and creating a new queue when there is no place on an existing queue. The second phase is an ideal merge in which the item to be removed is determined by keeping the queues in a priority queue .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: unshufflsort

context_nodes.label: upper triangular matrix
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines upper triangular matrix as: A matrix that is only defined at (i,j) when i ≤ j.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: upperTriangularMatrix

context_nodes.label: van Emde-Boas priority queue
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines van Emde-Boas priority queue as: An efficient implementation of priority queues where insert, delete, get minimum, get maximum, etc. take O(log log N) time, where N is the total possible number of keys . Depending on the circumstance, the implementation is null (if the queue is empty), an integer (if the queue has one integer), a bit vector of size N (if N is small), or a special data structure : an array of priority queues, called the bottom queues, and one more priority queue of array indexes of the bottom queues.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: vanemdeboas

context_nodes.label: vehicle routing problem
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines vehicle routing problem as: Find an optimal route of one or more vehicles through a graph . Also known as VRP.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: vehicleRouting

context_nodes.label: Vitter's algorithm
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Vitter's algorithm as: An adaptive Huffman coding scheme. Typically this produces codings the same length as or shorter than static Huffman coding . In the worst case , this uses one more bit per codeword .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: vittersAlgorithm

context_nodes.label: weighted, directed graph
context_nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines weighted, directed graph as: A directed graph that has a weight, or numeric value, associated with each edge .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: weightedDigraph

support.quote: The unification of gravity and quantum mechanics remains one of the most profound open questions in science. With recent advances in quantum technology, an experimental idea first proposed by Richard Feynman is now regarded as a promising route to testing this unification for the first time. The experiment involves placing a massive object in a quantum superposition of two locations and letting it gravitationally interact with another mass. If the two objects subsequently become entangled, this is considered unambiguous evidence that gravity obeys the laws of quantum mechanics.

canonical_record.label: Classical gravity plus QFT entanglement
canonical_record.summary: Aziz and Howl propose that extending the treatment of matter to quantum field theory permits a classical gravitational interaction to transmit quantum information and generate entanglement. Gundhi, Infantino and Bassi dispute the gravitational interpretation of the reported entanglement, attributing it to particle diffusion and free evolution for the partition considered.

support.quote: Here, we extend the description of the gravitational interaction used in these theorems to the full framework of quantum field theory, finding that theories with classical gravity can then transmit quantum information, and thus generate entanglement through physical, local processes. The effect scales differently to that predicted by theories of quantum gravity, providing information on the parameters and form of the experiment required to robustly evidence the quantum nature of gravity.

A recent paper published in Nature [Nature,646,813(2025)] claims that quantum particles become entangled through their gravitational interaction, even when the gravitational potential is classical. Here we show that the entanglement found by the authors is a consequence of letting particles diffuse from one object to the other. When this is not allowed, the wavefunction remains factorized. In fact, noticing that entanglement is relative to a chosen partition of the Hilbert space, we show that the choice of partition implicitly made by the authors is such that entanglement arises as soon as particles diffuse, even when no interaction potential is present. Therefore, it is the free evolution, not the classical gravitational potential, which acts as the entangling mechanism in the scenario considered by the authors.

canonical_record.summary: Rovelli and Smolin study nonperturbative quantum gravity using states defined in both loop and connection representations, with a basis labelled by generalized spin networks.

support.quote: We introduce a new basis on the state space of non-perturbative quantum gravity. The states of this basis are linearly independent, are well defined in both the loop representation and the connection representation, and are labeled by a generalization of Penrose's spin netoworks. The new basis fully reduces the spinor identities (SU(2) Mandelstam identities) and simplifies calculations in non-perturbative quantum gravity. In particular, it allows a simple expression for the exact solutions of the Hamiltonian constraint (Wheeler-DeWitt equation) that have been discovered in the loop representation. Since the states in this basis diagnolize operators that represent the three geometry of space, such as the area and volumes of arbitrary surfaces and regions, these states provide a discrete picture of quantum geometry at the Planck scale.

support.quote:
The causal set theory (CST) approach to quantum gravity postulates that at the most fundamental level, spacetime is discrete, with the spacetime continuum replaced by locally finite posets or "causal sets". The partial order on a causal set represents a proto-causality relation while local finiteness encodes an intrinsic discreteness. In the continuum approximation the former corresponds to the spacetime causality relation and the latter to a fundamental spacetime atomicity, so that finite volume regions in the continuum contain only a finite number of causal set elements. CST is deeply rooted in the Lorentzian character of spacetime, where a primary role is played by the causal structure poset. Importantly, the assumption of a fundamental discreteness in CST does not violate local Lorentz invariance in the continuum approximation. On the other hand, the combination of discreteness and Lorentz invariance gives rise to a characteristic non-locality which distinguishes CST from most other approaches to quantum gravity.
In this review we give a broad, semi-pedagogical introduction to CST, highlighting key results as well as some of the key open questions. This review is intended both for the beginner student in quantum gravity as well as more seasoned researchers in the field.

We report on a search for weakly interacting massive particle (WIMP) dark matter (DM) via elastic DM-xenon-nucleus interactions in the XENONnT experiment. We combine datasets from the first and second science campaigns resulting in a total exposure of 3.1 tonne-years. In a blind analysis of nuclear recoil events with energies above $3.8\,\mathrm{keV_{NR}}$, we find no significant excess above background. We set new upper limits on the spin-independent WIMP-nucleon scattering cross section for WIMP masses above $10\,\mathrm{GeV}/c^2$ with a minimum of $1.7\,\times\,10^{-47}\,\mathrm{cm^2}$ at $90\,\%$ confidence level for a WIMP mass of $30\,\mathrm{GeV}/c^2$. We achieve a best median sensitivity of $1.4\,\times\,10^{-47}\,\mathrm{cm^2}$ for a $41\,\mathrm{GeV}/c^2$ WIMP. Compared to the result from the first XENONnT science dataset, we improve our sensitivity by a factor of up to 1.8.

support.quote: We report on a search for weakly interacting massive particle (WIMP) dark matter (DM) via elastic DM-xenon-nucleus interactions in the XENONnT experiment. We combine datasets from the first and second science campaigns resulting in a total exposure of 3.1 tonne-years. In a blind analysis of nuclear recoil events with energies above $3.8\,\mathrm{keV_{NR}}$, we find no significant excess above background. We set new upper limits on the spin-independent WIMP-nucleon scattering cross section for WIMP masses above $10\,\mathrm{GeV}/c^2$ with a minimum of $1.7\,\times\,10^{-47}\,\mathrm{cm^2}$ at $90\,\%$ confidence level for a WIMP mass of $30\,\mathrm{GeV}/c^2$. We achieve a best median sensitivity of $1.4\,\times\,10^{-47}\,\mathrm{cm^2}$ for a $41\,\mathrm{GeV}/c^2$ WIMP. Compared to the result from the first XENONnT science dataset, we improve our sensitivity by a factor of up to 1.8.

Compared to electronic recoils (ERs), mainly expected from backgrounds, nuclear recoils (NRs) from WIMP scattering feature smaller S2/S1 ratios, allowing for ER/NR discrimination

support.quote: Three of the fundamental forces result from the exchange of force-carrier particles, which belong to a broader group called “bosons”. Particles of matter transfer discrete amounts of energy by exchanging bosons with each other. Each fundamental force has its own corresponding boson – the strong force is carried by the “gluon”, the electromagnetic force is carried by the “photon”, and the “W and Z bosons” are responsible for the weak force. Although not yet found, the “graviton” should be the corresponding force-carrying particle of gravity. The Standard Model includes the electromagnetic, strong and weak forces and all their carrier particles, and explains well how these forces act on all of the matter particles. However, the most familiar force in our everyday lives, gravity, is not part of the Standard Model, as fitting gravity comfortably into this framework has proved to be a difficult challenge. The quantum theory used to describe the micro world, and the general theory of relativity used to describe the macro world, are difficult to fit into a single framework. No one has managed to make the two mathematically compatible in the context of the Standard Model. But luckily for particle physics, when it comes to the minuscule scale of particles, the effect of gravity is so weak as to be negligible. Only when matter is in bulk, at the scale of the human body or of the planets for example, does the effect of gravity dominate. So the Standard Model still works well despite its reluctant exclusion of one of the fundamental forces.

support.quote: Black holes are among the most mysterious cosmic objects, much studied but not fully understood. These objects aren’t really holes. They’re huge concentrations of matter packed into very tiny spaces. A black hole is so dense that gravity just beneath its surface, the event horizon, is strong enough that nothing – not even light – can escape. The event horizon isn’t a surface like Earth’s or even the Sun’s. It’s a boundary that contains all the matter that makes up the black hole.

support.quote:
How do particles get mass?
Particles get their mass by interacting with the Higgs field; they do not have a mass of their own.
The stronger a particle interacts with the Higgs field, the heavier the particle ends up being. Photons, for example, do not interact with this field and therefore have no mass. Yet other elementary particles, including electrons, quarks and bosons, do interact and hence have a variety of masses.
This mass-giving interaction with the Higgs field is known as the Brout-Englert-Higgs mechanism, proposed by theorists Robert Brout, François Englert and Peter Higgs.
